summary_of_change:
Through this operations update No. 1, the Venezuelan Red Cross aims to inform about:
- A no cost timeframe extension of 3 months (new end date: 28 February 2025).

Significant progress has been made in this operation, with an implementation rate of 65% to date. However, delays in the arrival of medicines and health supplies have hindered the health strategy's progress. While procurement processes began early in the operation and efforts have been made to expedite them, health-related procurement is classified as 'special procurement,' leading to delays. Both local and regional procurement processes are expected to conclude by the second week of November.

A three-month no-cost extension will enable the completion of pending activities, enhance the National Society's capacity, and support preparations for potential social conflicts anticipated in January 2025, coinciding with the country’s next presidential inauguration.
icrc:
The ICRC Delegation in Caracas works in the states with areas affected by armed violence (Apure, Aragua, Bolivar, Zulia, Tachira, Capital District) offering protection activities, assistance and developing dialogue activities with the Venezuelan authorities and the country's security forces. It is currently cooperating with the CRV in projects on Security Management, Safer Access, RFL, Protection, PPAA, and Communication (Visibility), among others. In the post-electoral context, the ICRC maintains its humanitarian access in the country, as well as its dialogue with authorities to offer services in terms of Detention, RFL, and Health. ICRC has collaborated with the VRC for the activation of 22 Situation Rooms during the electoral and post-electoral phases. It has continuously guided and advised on the construction of the contingency plan and security guidelines, closely coordinating the management of public communication and sharing key messages to be delivered to the community, volunteers, etc.

Within the framework of Movement coordination and following its close support to the VRC during its restructuring process, the ICRC actively participates in coordination spaces with the other partners present in the country, at strategic and technical levels. Security roundtables take place regularly, where all partners share information and analyze the context together, producing security recommendations for all teams on the field.
selection_criteria:
- People physically or psychologically affected during or after situations of civil unrest    
- People separated from family members or acquaintances due to these situations.   
- People with mobility limitations or affected by cuts in connectivity services.   
- People with chronic illnesses who do not have access to medication due to limitations in the provision of health services.   
- Volunteers and staff of the VRC or other agencies involved in the response.   

Within these groups, priority will be given to older adults, children, adolescents, pregnant women and persons with disabilities due to their specific needs and vulnerabilities, which require special attention to ensure an equitable and effective humanitarian response aligned with the humanitarian principles of the VRC. In addition, ensuring staff security will be essential to maintain response capacity and protect those providing assistance.​
ifrc:
​​Through the Head of Delegation, the Security Officer and the Programme and Operations Unit, the Country Office has provided support and coordination to the National Society's core team in the review and activation of its contingency plan and activation of different mechanisms. Close coordination has also been maintained with the technical areas at the Americas level to ensure synergies between context updates, scenario analysis, and support that the National Society may require. 

​​Communication with stakeholders has also been maintained to ensure and enhance communication of further actions taken at national level.
risk_security_concern:
​​It is imperative to improve the identification and visibility of the volunteers and humanitarian personnel involved by providing them with identification elements, such as uniforms, to comply with Operational Security (OS) standards.

Guidance material, such as an Operational Security pocket guide, can facilitate the strict application of standards and guidelines in emergency contexts and assist the steam on the ground in this operation. OS advice and technical support will be provided to volunteers and humanitarian staff through the socialization of guidelines for this context, to ensure a rigorous application of the OS standards and Safer Access, which all activated humanitarian staff will implement. The VRC has operational security protocols and team monitoring and tracking mechanisms in place. A Security Protocol for volunteer and staff activities will be developed and implemented.

​Furthermore, due to the volatility of the context, operations and security units from both VRC and IFRC Country Delegation (CD) will constantly monitor the evolution of the scenarios to mitigate the possible impacts on the operation and personnel. Ensuring clear external communications will be a key factor to guarantee the protection of RCRC personnel within the country. Hence, coordination and communication flow between VRC, IFRC, ICRC, GRC is established.
national_authorities: ​​National Authorities convened the National Defense Council and activated the security plan, deploying security forces throughout the country, with a special focus on areas that have seen the highest number of demonstrations and social unrest. Strict monitoring from the authorities is being held.​
communication:
In an environment of social tension, it is crucial that the Venezuelan Red Cross maintains trust, integrity and awareness of its action. For this reason, the Communication Department developed a Communication Plan whose main objective is to preserve and strengthen the role of the VRC, respect for the emblem and compliance with the Principles, while ensuring the safety and well-being of its volunteers and teams.

This plan focuses on internal coordination between the heads of delegations, the dissemination of messages on social networks and, in the media, a list of key messages for volunteers and the training of volunteers in communication and media management. This was shared with each branch.

Specific objectives included

1. Positioning the VRC in its auxiliary and compliance role on social networks and in the media.
2. Promote the good use of the Venezuelan Red Cross emblem internally and externally.
surge_personnel_deployed:
In coordination with the Venezuelan Red Cross, and taking into account the context and needs, two persons were deployed.
 
- The Operations Coordinator, for two months, to review and support the National Society in reviewing security analyses and scenarios, providing operational security training, training for the development and updating of the National Society's security plan, reviewing situation rooms and crisis procedures, and providing ongoing support for activities in coordination with the National Society.
 
- The Mental Health and Psychosocial Support Officer for one month, providing support to ensure the implementation of a MHPSS work plan, including activities such as: providing training and forming psychosocial response teams as part of the response, reviewing MHPSS interventions in emergency situations, and reviewing the National Society's MHPSS strategy.
 
The regional team provided support to ensure optimal and timely deployments, taking into account entry visa restrictions and commercial flight restrictions that increase deployment costs.
partner_national_society: ​​The German Red Cross (GRC) has supported the National Society at headquarters and in six branches, providing resources to cover operational expenses related to food for volunteers and staff involved in the actions. In addition, it has provided medical supplies and medicines from the MOFA-supported project, which is being implemented in collaboration with the National Society.​
event_scope:
The post-electoral context has maintained an atmosphere of social tension in the country. Demonstrations began on 29 July. In just two days, 564 protests were registered nationwide, according to secondary sources. Furthermore, National Authorities have confirmed over 2,000 people detained and that 77 security officers have been injured within only 5 days. However, no official figures on the number of the people injured or killed have been published. This situation of insecurity has resulted in a reduction in the number of spontaneous manifestations and social clashes. The national authority has maintained the deployment of security forces throughout the country and has initiated investigations to identify and prosecute those responsible for acts of violence and vandalism. Additionally, it was announced the construction of two new maximum-security ”re-education centers".

Both parties, the Government and opposition have continued to call for rallies and marches, some of which have escalated into protests leaving people injured in cities such as Maracaibo, Maracay, Valencia, Caracas, Guanare, Valle de la Pascua, Coro, Barcelona, and others. Popular areas of the Capital and several states of the country have also maintained active protests throughout the days.

The Public Prosecutor's Office has announced that leaders of the opposition will be prosecuted for several charges, including usurpation of functions, dissemination of false information, incitement to disobey the law, association to commit a crime, and conspiracy, after the opposition party published the results of the 28 July elections independently.

In this sense, the international community has requested to comply with the guarantees of the voting process, requesting the delivery of evidence to the population that supports the result reported by the authorities. As of 5 August, diplomatic relations with Argentina, Chile, Costa Rica, Panama, Peru, Dominican Republic, and Uruguay have been broken. While commercial flights to Panama, Peru, and the Dominican Republic have been suspended. Furthermore, the US and Costa Rica have officially recognized the opposition leader as the new president, which can lead to additional tensions.

The massive dissemination of news on social networks has brought about situations of alert and fear in part of the population, causing significant collective stress. Surveillance of the media and social networks has been intensified to disseminate the news. National authorities have blamed social media as a provoker of violence in Venezuela. This situation has generated difficulty for the population to access safe and verified information.

In a context of growing social unrest, monetary fluctuations such as the rise of the dollar, which according to the Central Bank of Venezuela increased by 11% in October alone, and the country's public health system, which lacks the resources to care for patients and the number of ambulances to respond to mass casualty emergencies, materials, supplies and medicines are not sufficient. 

Moreover, this situation has created the risk of a new wave of migration in the coming months if the context does not improve, with an increase in the number of people on the move, which could seriously affect humanitarian needs not only in the border states but also in neighboring countries, as has been the case in recent years.
human_resource:
A total of 200 volunteers, distributed among the 13 priority branches, are part of this operation. This includes first responders and health personnel who served the emergency.
 
In addition, this operation was supported by two full-time technicians who managed the plan according to the following profile:
- A project coordinator, who managed the implementation of the plan with the technical areas prioritised by the National Society, ensuring compliance with the VRC and IFRC guidelines and instruments within the established deadlines, as well as, ensuring coordination both internally and with the IFRC and ICRC on National Society actions.
 
- The National Society MHPSS officer received support from Surge in the general capacity assessment of the team, implementing and developing activities (trainings, accompaniment, revision of didactic material) related to this area, working in alignment with the National Health Directorate.
 
In addition, an administrative assistant has provided support to ensure adequate accountability and administrative progress internally for the implementation of activities.
title: Venezuela: Civil Unrest
logistic_capacity_of_ns: Procurement processes were carried out through the IFRC Country Office Procurement Unit and the Regional Logistics Office, taking into account available supplies. Local procurement and procurement with the regional team was carried out mainly due to the nature of the purchase (health supplies). This process was evaluated in detail by the Regional Logistics Unit team and the Procurement Officer together with the operations Coordinator to ensure compliance with established procedures, as the availability of local suppliers is very limited.
un_or_other_actor: At the local level, the Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) has comprehensively monitored the evolution of the context, analyzing the different scenarios that could develop in the upcoming weeks. The Contingency Plan was activated, and meetings have been held with the HCT both before and after the elections. In addition, local organizations such as Monitor de Víctimas and Foro Penal have continuously been monitoring the number of affectations.
response_strategy:
Since the activation of the National Society's Electoral Contingency Plan, the VRC has maintained an impartial position during the different events, respecting the Fundamental Principles that guide its actions. 

Although the national electoral process has ended, the demonstrations of 29 July continue and have a serious impact on the Venezuelan population, an effect that is enhanced by the complex pre-existing socio-economic crisis. Therefore, the VRC determined the activation of this DREF based on the possible scenarios foreseen for the coming weeks, due to the political tensions and the volatile context observed, to provide services to the population and prepare for an escalation of events. The strategy has been designed considering the context of the country, and previous experiences in similar operations in 2014 and 2019, which have involved different lines of institutional action and advocacy with the authorities and humanitarian actors. 

Health: 

Pre Hospital Care - First Aid services:
In situations of violence, immediate intervention can be the difference between life and death. In this sense the VRC will reinforce the knowledge of technical staff and volunteers in first aid, prehospital care as well as to adapt previous experiences to the current context. Refreshment will be made through the development BEC courses (Basic Emergency Course), which is an advanced training and closer to what a volunteer needs when attending to a wounded person as a result of a violent trauma. Coordination with the ICRC will be carried out as it has already provided training in these areas, and the VRC has instructors that could replicate in the prioritized branches.

Furthermore, the VRC will provide first aid and pre-hospital care services to reduce human suffering, prevent long-term complications and ensure an efficient and coordinated response. For this reason, once the teams are prepared and equipped, first aid and PHC will be provided at VRC health centers or as part of first responses during protests.

In this sense, assisting the population at the moment and having the capacity to transfer them to health centres is a key need for which the VRC will ensure that essential medical equipment is available in the ambulances. In this regard, it is proposed to reinforce the ambulance services of 10 branches that have the units with the provision of essential medical supplies such as emergency kits, bleeding kits and mechanical replenishments such as bandages, gauze, physiological solution, among others. The service of these units will be made available as needed through coordination with local authorities and public health centers in the area. In addition, primary health care attention will be given, when possible, at community level with a strong focus on areas where access to health has reduced as a consequence of the context. If at community level is not possible, activities will be carried out either at VRC or in the nearest public health center. 
 
Mental Health and Psychological Support 
Throughout the operation, the Venezuelan Red Cross contemplates the refreshment sessions on psychosocial support response teams as well as to review its strategy and implementation plan on MHPPS actions in this type of contexts. This review process will be carried out by MHPSS technical personnel jointly with the technical team and the National Health Direction. Furthermore, dissemination of key messages to the population regarding mental health care will be provided. 

Offering psychosocial support to the people affected as well as to volunteers is crucial to reduce stress and anxiety related to the exposure of these events and can help prevent long-term psychological disorders such as post-traumatic stress disorder and improve response capacity through clearer and faster decisions. In addition, these actions reinforce morale and team spirit by transmitting support and solidarity, helping to prevent burnout and promoting recovery and resilience. For this reason, these services will be available, and it is expected that they will reach at least 650 people including VRC volunteers and the population. 

Protection, gender and inclusion (PGI): 

Restoring Family Links: 
Through its RFL program, the Venezuelan Red Cross will provide RFL services to at least 250 people through connectivity points, if the context demands it. These services will include facilitating communication through phone calls or messages and organizing reunions where possible. Coordination with the ICRC will be held. The RFL programme has been in place since 2015, with a division of roles between the VRC and the ICRC for case management: Detention and Armed Conflict or Armed Violence is an ICRC-only portfolio. 

Dissemination of key messages on PGI 
The dissemination of key messages on PGI is critical in ensuring the safety and dignity of all individuals during civil unrest. The VRC will implement a comprehensive communication strategy to spread awareness on how mitigate protection risks, preventing gender-based violence, and promoting inclusivity. These messages will be disseminated through social media, ensuring broad reach and understanding. By fostering an environment of respect and inclusion, we aim to prevent discrimination and violence in this already convulsed context. 

Furthermore, VRC will carry out webinars or short refreshment sessions on key topics such as principles of protection in context of armed violence/ civil unrest, gender sensitivity, implications of an internal security crisis from a PGI approach. 

Community Engagement and accountability (CEA): 

Implement Feedback Mechanisms 
In situations of social demonstrations, maintaining open lines of communication with the public is essential for ensuring that the response is effective and meets the needs of the population. To this end, the Venezuelan Red Cross will collect inputs on the services provided through satisfaction surveys. Furthermore, collection of rumors and concerns from the population will be gathered to understand people's perception on the evolution of the context and clarify them through key messages on social media. These mechanisms will be designed by CEA focal point, disseminating how to properly implement it and analyze de information gathered. These actions will be implemented, when possible, after the provision of services guaranteeing the anonymity. 

National Society Strengthening: 

Operational Security  
In the context of civil unrest, ensuring the safety of volunteers working in potentially vulnerable environments is of utmost importance. The VRC will provide operational safety refresher training. This training will cover security protocols, risk assessment and emergency procedures tailored to the challenges of volatile situations. By enhancing their ability to manage and mitigate risks, the training aims to ensure the safety and well-being of volunteers during operations. In addition, constant monitoring and analysis of the evolution of the context will be held. A security plan is in place, which could be reviewed, as well as an update of the Movement's contingency plan for civil unrest. 

Furthermore, in order to improve preparedness and response capacity, key processes such as situation rooms, data analysis, development of key reports, crisis rooms and contingency plans, scenario analysis will be reviewed to ensure that volunteers are well prepared to deal with unexpected situations and can contribute to a coordinated and effective response for real-time decision making. 
 
Implementation of a Communications Plan 
Effective communication is crucial for a coordinated response in emergency situations. The VRC will implement a comprehensive Communications Plan to streamline internal and external communications during social manifestations. This plan will establish clear protocols for information dissemination, ensure timely updates to all stakeholders, and facilitate efficient coordination among branches. The goal is to enhance the overall communication strategy, improving the flow of information and ensuring that all team members are aligned and informed. 

Development of key messages focused on Red Cross Red Crescent Movement, auxiliar role of the National Society, respect for the emblem, protection and prevention actions will be held with a strong focus on protection. Visibility of vehicles will be included ensuring their recognition and protection during emergency operations. The VRC will undertake the identification of 10 vehicles to ensure they are clearly identified as Red Cross assets, maintaining the safety of vehicles and their occupants, as well as reinforcing the legitimacy of the Red Cross’s presence and activities in affected areas. 

Understanding the principles of Movement doctrine and mastering operational communication are vital for effective humanitarian action. Educational sessions for 200 volunteers on Movement Doctrine and Operational Communication will be developed through the National Direction. These sessions will cover the core values and operational standards of the Red Cross Movement, as well as best practices for communicating during operations. By deepening volunteers' understanding of these principles, the sessions aim to improve adherence to Red Cross standards and enhance overall operational efficiency. Furthermore, it is contemplated to develop a session on humanitarian diplomacy and auxiliary roles to board members in branches.

Provision of Protective and Visibility Equipment to volunteers 
To ensure the safety and visibility of volunteers in the field, the VRC will provide protective and visibility uniforms for 200 volunteers for safeguarding volunteers from physical harm and ensuring they are easily identifiable in complex environments, thus enhancing their safety and effectiveness during operations.
people_assisted: Through this operation, the VRC aims to reach 2,600 people by providing first aid services, prehospital care, MHPSS care, and primary health care within communities affected by severe social demonstrations and promoting key messages focused on the permanent diffusion of the Fundamental Principles, the good use of the emblem, the Code of Conduct and Red Cross actions in situations of violence. In addition, it is expected to increase local capacities of 200 volunteers in the branches prioritized. This figure was calculated by taking into account the VRC's previous experience during demonstrations in 2019, as well as the information collected by the National Society on incidents of violence.
operation_objective:
Through this IFRC-DREF operation, the Venezuelan Red Cross aims to provide immediate assistance to at least 2,600 people through the implementation of activities under prehospital care (PHC), first aid, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), and Restoring Family Links (RFL) to people directly affected by civil unrest for a period of six months (3-month extension). 

As of the writing of this operations update, 13 VRC branches have been prioritized: Aragua, Amazonas, Anzoátegui, Carabobo, Barinas, Distrito Capital, Falcón, Guárico, Lara, Mérida, Nueva Esparta, Portuguesa, and Trujillo. This prioritization is based on estimates indicating areas where protests are likely to be recorded, as these are locations of principal cities with a history of protests. In addition, it has been considered the inclusion of Guárico, Portuguesa and Amazonas states as severe protests took place after the elections in 2024, having as a result sever number of people affected.
pmer:
Through the Delegation in Venezuela involved in the operation, monitoring was carried out to ensure the implementation of the operation and the progress of the actions. To this end, monitoring missions were carried out in the branches prioritised according to the context, accompanied by the local team and SURGE, as well as the Regional Security Office team and other areas.

Given the volatility of the context, the teams in charge of implementing the operation will continuously monitor the situation, including risk analysis and relevant mitigation measures at different points of the operation. In addition, the IFRC's technical security staff in CD and ARO will provide continuous support in the follow-up of the security phases. 

Through the National Society team and in collaboration with the IFRC PMER Officer, a monitoring plan and follow-up meetings with the IFRC Coordinator have been developed to properly systematize progress and constraints encountered in order to address them efficiently.
major_coordination_mechanism:
​​At the request of the National Society, the Movement's coordination table was activated on 30 July to ensure the exchange of information and identify possible actions for both the National Society and its partners in the country. Constant communication is maintained at both strategic and operational levels between the VRC, the IFRC, the ICRC and the GRC. 

​​The VRC will coordinate the revision and updating of the Movement Contingency Plan for Civil Unrest which was approved in 2017 and later reviewed in 2019.
event_description:
On 28 July 2024, Venezuela held presidential elections called by the National Electoral Council (CNE), the national institution in charge of the electoral process. On 29 July at 01:00, the CNE declared the ruling party's candidate the winner. The opposition immediately rejected the results, claiming to have received more than 60% of the popular vote. However, at 11:00 a.m. of the same day, the government candidate was declared re-elected president by the CNE, triggering a series of social demonstrations in 17 of the 23 states of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela. 

On 29 July, the opposition claimed to have won more than 70% of the votes cast. Later that day, the opposition informed the Venezuelan people and the international community that it had published, through a website, the election results per voting table that supported this claim.

The international community issued a majority statement calling on the electoral body to publish the election results, demanding transparency in the presentation of the evidence supporting the result announced by the authorities. Subsequently, the Supreme Court of Justice issued a statement confirming the results announced by the National Electoral Council.

On 5 August, the Venezuelan government broke off diplomatic relations with Argentina, Chile, Costa Rica, Panama, Peru, the Dominican Republic and Uruguay. Commercial flights to Panama, Peru and the Dominican Republic were suspended. At the same time, demonstrations and protests continued with varying degrees of intensity in different cities across the country. The country was also hit by road blockades, which affected trade and led to shortages in small local grocery stores and large supermarket chains, particularly of perishable goods such as vegetables.

In response, President Nicolás Maduro convened the National Defense Council and activated a security plan that includes the deployment of security forces throughout the country, with a particular focus on areas with the highest number of demonstrations and social unrest. The national government has already reported more than 2,000 arrests of demonstrators, and there are no official figures on the number of injured and dead. As of 5 August, local organizations such as Monitor de Víctimas, Foro Penal and Provea reported 93 injured and 24 dead.

While the first few weeks after the elections were marked by the greatest disturbances, the frequency of spontaneous demonstrations and calls for rallies or marches by the opposition leadership and the government decreased in September and October. 

However, the political conflict is not over: the inauguration of the president-elect is constitutionally scheduled for 10 January. Analysts agree that this milestone could mark an upsurge in public unrest as both candidates, opposition candidate Edmundo González and Nicolás Maduro, struggle for international recognition after declaring themselves the winners of the last electoral process. This dispute, in the context of a highly polarized and expectant country, could generate an upsurge in demonstrations, protests and public unrest in the country in early 2025.

Through the DREF election preparedness, CVM managed to deliver first aid and stay safe trainings to volunteers across all provinces of the country. These volunteers were active in the pre electoral period, and during voting day. Staff from CVM continue monitoring protests and demonstrations to deploy more trained volunteers to provide first aid services where applicable, as well as ensure the ambulances are ready for deployment. From previous operations and programs, the NS has provided multiple First Aid and Community Based health care and first aid trainings across the country. For the 2023 municipal elections, 12 previously trained volunteers in first aid deployed in Maputo to provide first aid support. This year, with the support of Belgian Red Cross, 45 volunteers have been trained in first aid. Other volunteers that have previously been trained, or newly identified volunteers, need to receive refresher trainings on first aid as well as be properly equipped to deliver services during the electoral period of 2024. 

The NS has also made an inventory of the stock they will require as well as the volunteers available in the targeted areas, through the volunteer management system, it is guaranteed to have volunteers on standby in case further support is required.. This information can be found below in the operational strategy section.

needs_identified.title: protection_gender_and_inclusion
needs_identified.description:
In the event of the demonstrations, people already in vulnerable situations have found themselves in worse situations. People with specific needs including pregnant and lactating women, people with disabilities, and the elderly. During the current demonstrations, road blocks and lack of public transportation limited access of pregnant woman to the hospital for example. Those waiting in line with young children and the elderly were more prone to be dehydrated and requiring first aid support. 

Volunteers will need to be trained on the code of conduct and PGI issues, especially on the prevention of gender-based violence, in order to protect themselves, and to better assist the most vulnerable. This operation will aim at reducing the risk factors for an increase in gender-based violence, identify GVB and PSEA cases and treat/refer them.

needs_identified.title: health
needs_identified.description:
Election campaign rallies, demonstrations, voting days, period of results in hotspot areas have lead to violence which has resulted in injuries, deaths, separation of family members, and significant psychological effects.  With the ongoing strike and manifestations, population in these high-risk areas need support in terms of first aid care, medical evacuations, and referral to hospitals in the event of serious cases. Additionally, the march is asking people to move large distances from provinces to the capital city, meaning that main roads may experience blockages and people walking or travelling long distances may have some health needs along the way. Secondary impacts of the manifestations are also impacting health of the broader population, including those who can not access health care due to lack of transportation and road blocks, as well as those that cannot access food or pharmacies during the shutdowns of businesses and lack of stock once businesses have reopened. 

Prepositioning of first aid kits and other equipment will be needed in order to ensure the continued and full capacity of NS in the event of an escalation of tensions, as well as the protection of NS staff and volunteers. Volunteers will need to be trained or refreshed on basic first aid and psychological first aid as one of the requirements during this operation.

needs_identified.title: community_engagement_and_accountability
needs_identified.description:
At all times, but especially during elections, it is important to sensitize communities and all political forces on the mandate, role, mission, and principles of the Red Cross, but also on the mechanism to put in place, while laying emphasis the principles of neutrality and impartiality. In past electoral times, there have been confusions with RC volunteers wearing red shirts that could be seen as affiliated with one of the political parties. In this elections, there are reports of volunteers having to explain the role of the RC in order to gain safe access through an area. 

To this effect, the volunteers will need to be re-briefed on RC movement mandate, role and principles and train in safety and security. Visibility materials (vests, ID cards, bibs, stickers, and flags) need to be made available to the branches for security and visibility purposes, both playing an essential role in this type of intervention.

summary_of_change: operational strategy changes as this is scaling up the DREF from Prepardness to Response. The original prepardness DREF was completed successfully, and the trigger to the scenario of increase of demostrations was met. This scenario has brought new security and humanitarian risks and needs. On Nov 7th, the largest protest took place as the culmination of a 7 day strike, requiring further support and an operational scale up. This day is the trigger for the scale up. The NS response plan was devised with a new set of risk scenarios (from minimal further disturbances, ongoing protests, and escalation into full civil unrest). The most likely scenario (ongoing protest) is being used to move forward with a response plan. The target population has been updated with more accurate data on reach of volunteers involved in first aid activities during the prepardness phase, and now is aligned with the response strategy that has a specific reach per first aid unit for the number of days it is activated. The request for a change in budget/second allocation is based on the need for the scale up to response which requires further communications, first aid supplies, security assessments, volunteer incentives, and field coordination support to allow for first aid response to affected populations as per the new operational strategy. As well as preparedness and response elements for similar events in the coming days or weeks. Timeframe extended to allow for time after things calm down to do workshops and lessons learned activities.
identified_gaps: Based on how the opposition party suggests to be the follow up from the 7 day strike, various different scenarios could be at play. An internal IFRC humanitarian scenario analysis has been developed showing different scenarios and their likelihoods. These scenarios have triggers to ensure we can escalate or de-escalate the response as needed as each scenario has potential to give rise to new humanitarian needs.
icrc: ICRC has been involved in the election contingency plans and have been part of conversations with NS about potential support they can provide to the Electoral Contingency Plan. They have committed funds for during and after election activities as well as in-kind items (bibs, hats, and flags) to the Contingency Plan. The funding contributes to the broader contingency plan. The DREF complements these efforts. Together, ICRC and IFRC funds covered the training of 55 ToTs and 1100 volunteers. ICRC straongly focuses in country in Cabo Delgado province due to the ongoing conflict, the support to the contingency plan is not limited to Cabo Delgado but could cover Cabo Delgado as a key hotspot for potential violence. ICRC has supported training of volunteers in Cabo Delgado and Nampula on safe access, and also support with the insurance of the volunteers. ICRC and IFRC are in constant communication over security assessments and further support to CVM and are planning to contribute to the response plan. Final commitment to response plan will be confirmed in following days.
selection_criteria:
Referring to geographical selection criteria, the highest hotspots districts known by experience for potential violence before, during and later after the elections will be prioritized, including urban high-density areas and areas with strong links to political campaign representatives across all 11 provinces.

Focus on reaching and ensuring wellbeing of most vulnerable people (pregnant and lactating women, the elderly, people with disabilities, minority groups, the sick people, the injured people, etc

Much attention will be put on detecting sexual gender-based violence and providing referrals.
ifrc: IFRC has been in contact with CVM and coordinating with Movement partners regarding the status of the electoral campaign and assessing coverage and coordinating support to the contingency and response plan developed by the CVM. IFRC has also supported providing security trainings, with additional briefings to the Movement and developed election contingency plans and is managing risks related to potential violence. Upon request of the NS, IFRC has launched a DREF for Electoral Preparedness and supported NS in implementing the DREF including through the deployment of a security focal point to Mozambique to support safe access trainings for volunteers and security assessments, as well as external coordination with UN and other stakeholders. IFRC has supported the development of NSs readiness and response plan, from which this DREF scale-up is requested.
risk_security_concern: During times of electoral or political crisis, security becomes a big concern. This is particularly the case  in urban areas, where the situation can escalate to violence. Security threats can include demonstrations, spontaneous or planned riots, robbery and vandalism, followed by severe violence, roadblocks by demonstrators or security forces, attacks among parties’ members, etc. The security situation will be assessed regularly among the Red Cross Partners (NS, IFRC and ICRC) for exchanges of information on security and necessary measures that need to be taken. ICRC supports security in the conflict areas in the North of the country where IFRC does not have physical presence. NS will also communicate with the branches of the high-risk localities targeted in collaboration with the community authorities and will provide regular updates on the situation. To reduce the risk of RCRC personnel falling victim to crime, violence, active risk mitigation measures must be adopted. Security orientation and briefing for all teams prior to deployment will also be undertaken to ensure the safety and security of response teams. Standard security protocols about general norms, cultural sensitivity, and an overall code of conduct will be put in place. Minimum security requirements will be strictly maintained and applied to all NS staff and volunteers throughout the operation. Visibility material will be essential for all volunteers and staff in the field.
national_authorities:
The Provincial Government agency that organizes voting and statistical analysis is being contacted to make available the lists of the polling stations of all districts, which will allow the placement of teams in the Assemblies with the largest number of polling stations and those places suspected of probable disturbances. 
Contact have been made by NS with the Health authorities for actions integrated in Health coverage at all levels and the possibility of making medicines available for assistance will be seen.
communication: An appropriate communication strategy will be implemented prior to the operation, with four main objectives: Establish trust in the Red Cross to facilitate its actions and the care of victims. Enhance the visibility of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement by communicating its actions, mandate, and initiatives. Communicate on plans with government entities and to communities.
partner_national_society: Currently, Belgian RC and German RC, are looking to support the Response plan.  Belgian RC will contribute with fuel and first aid equipment (stretches and first aid kits). German RC will confirm contribution in following days. PNSs have contributed to the broader readiness and capacity building of the NS through ongoing long-term projects across the country. This year, Belgian Red Cross has trained 45 volunteers in first aid. Since 2022, Belgian RC has trained 450 volunteers in first aid.
event_scope:
Electoral processes have the potential to pose a threat in the pre- during and post-election periods, during campaigning, voting, and demonstrations. This election period in Mozambique is also marked by a number of socio-economic problems, including the El Nino induced drought and conflict in the north, floods, inflation, and others. Additionally, last year municipal elections brought conflicts that were unresolved and may break out further during this electoral period. Conflicts linked to the elections could increase the vulnerability of people already in need. During demonstrations and violence, markets, supermarkets, schools and other sources of income may remain closed, creating further food insecurity and socioeconomic concerns. Alternatively, these locations may be looted. Further conflicts could arise in rural areas. Long waiting lines during voting, participation in outdoor campaigns and demonstrations can impact vulnerable population and exacerbate health issues and gender-based violence particularly for children, elderly, people with disabilities, people who need to travel far to voting stations, and others. Young people and the poor may be manipulated into becoming involved in violence, creating a precarious situation, particularly for the poorest people, pregnant and breastfeeding women and the elderly. Sexual violence can also occur, particularly in isolated areas. 

Risk exposure: People that will be part of the demonstrations thus being exposed to harm following expected violence. People that go to vote. People that are involved in campaigning.  People indirectly exposed, that is voters or people willing to register themselves for the votes are likely be caught in violence during the rallies, and on voting days. This will concern all group ages.

Given the electoral timetable, the current situation, recent events and the background on violence after last year results that are expected to be amplified, the two month period of campaigning, voting, and releasing results of this process are likely to remain a sensitive period.  A likely period of localized but highly repetitive demonstrations and violence will be considered, as well as broader health and first aid support to those waiting to vote in long lines with no share, are as follows: Mid-september to October 9th (campaigning); October 9th (election day). One week period for counting votes and releasing results. October 15th -October 30th (demonstrations).  These time-periods were covered through the Prepardness DREF.

Since then, with no resolution of the election results, strikes and protests have continued for 7 days, culminating in an occupation of Maputo city on Nov 7th. This key date marked the need for an immediate response for the Nov 7th protest, as well as the development and implementation of different response plans based on renewed humanitarian situation analysis.

Expected recounting or delays in final result announcement would further expand the time period for demonstrations and could escalate violence. Demonstrations have been highest in urban areas.

Given that the violence situation was met in the preparedness phase, a new humanitarian and security analysis was performed that led to three new scenarios, each of which has its own 
 response plan to ensure NS can continue we delivering first aid to the population and ensure security for population as well as staff and volunteers across the extended turbulent post-election period. 

Scenario 1: Protest continue after Nov 7 with minimal hurt people. Disruptions end, incidents and protest decrease and no further protests take place for 1 week.
Scenario 2: Protest continue through the end of the year intermittently, with medium to significant number of injuries, but no further escalation.
Scenario 3: Onset of civil unrest due to large-scale political issues and long-term business closures.
More details in the operational strategy section.

title: Mozambique Election Readiness & Response
logistic_capacity_of_ns: The NS has mapped out the stock they already have that will be used and then need to be replenished. The DREF will provide funds for this procurement and replenishment, and ICRC will all be contributing to some items. The additional stock needed for scale up will be procured by IFRC or by PNSs through their contributions to the response operation.
un_or_other_actor: The UN agencies are active in the country and supports in coordination and identification of needs and capacities of humanitarian actors. HCT meetings continue. The European Union has deployed and Election Observation Mission to observe the elections.
response_strategy:
As this is a General Election, people of voting age will go to the polls, which can result in long hours of waiting, potentially causing indispositions that may require assistance. In addition, in some places, there may be situations of insecurity that sometimes result in injuries. Furthermore, violence can be expected in the period post the notification of the results, based on experience from pervious electoral years. 

Preparedness implementation strategy: 

The first phase (Preparedness DREF), based on NSs contingency planning for the electoral period, aims to train and equip 1100 volunteers across 5 districts of each of the 11 provinces in matters of First Aid, Safer Access and CEA to be able to provide first aid services during campaigning and voting day. The Preparedness DREF, alongside contributions from the ICRC, supports the training and equipping of 1100 of these volunteers. "Safer Access" as well as CEA approach and de-escalation of conflict and the provision of first aid remain the main focus of the prepardness phase, with training sessions at national, provincial and district levels for intervention teams. Training of trainers in First Aid and Safer Access at national level. These trainers, in turn, will replicate the training in 55 selected districts, with five participants per province (provincial secretaries, technicians, and three First Aid trainers).

In the lead up period to elections, volunteers will be actively engaged with key stakeholders of the communities and staff of CVM with political parties to promote peace keeping as well as clear understanding of RC movement during election period. Additionally, for quick sharing of information, escalation of issues identified in the field such as rumors, a communication tree has been established by CVM to ensure contact from volunteers in districts, to provincial, to HQ national level. 

During campaigning, voting day, and the weeks following the election, placement of a teams of two volunteers equipped with first aid kits, drinking water and disposable cups will be set up in assemblies with a larger number of tables. The teams will be positioned in strategic locations, away from the polling stations between 300 and 600 meters away from the polling stations, but visible, and other teams will circulate through the polling stations where the volunteers are not positioned. During any potential initial demonstration teams of NS staff and volunteers will patrol and monitor different areas and assess where it is safe to deploy volunteers to provide first aid services. Information will be communicated at the community level on where the closes point of first aid service can be found for those in need. The ambulances will also be ready to deploy with trained volunteers. 
  
Additionally the preparedness phase includes the procurement or replenishment of stock as follows (these numbers are separate and already take into consideration the items given by ICRC) which was done through the preparedness DREF. The NS ambulances will also be ready.

Bibs: replenish 390, procure 360
Kits: replenish 13, procure 97 
Flags: procure 72
Hats: procure 650

ICRC contributing through in-kind donations (350 bibs, 24 flags, and 350 hats) as well as funds (2M meticais) to complement gaps in funding of the broader preparedness plan.

The preparedness phase contains 2 scenarios, one of normal conditions and one of violence. 

Preparedness Non-violence Situation: Volunteers will engage community stakeholders before elections and provide support during election day with basic first aid to preserve wellbeing (e.g. dehydration, minor injuries, monitor violence, etc). Operation will end if after election results are announced if there are no demonstrations or calls for demonstrations for an entire week long period in the district volunteers are active in (1 week demonstration free post announcement of results)

Preparedness violence situation: Volunteers engaged through election day as per non-violence situation. Violence situation is activated based on notification of announcements from political parties for demonstrations and unsatisfaction post electoral results. This would indicate the volunteers are on stand-by and are activated throughout the immediate aftermath of the elections (up to 1 month through the month of October) or if there is 1 full week without protests of demonstrations or calls for demonstrations to continue providing first aid services to affected populations. If scenario 2 is met, this indicates the need for a new humanitarian scenario analysis and security assessments which will be used for the development of a response plan based on different escalation or de-escalation of violence scenarios.


Response implementation strategy:

Given that the situation was met in the preparedness phase, a new humanitarian and security analysis was performed that led to three new scenarios, each of which has its own response plan to ensure NS can continue we delivering first aid to the population and ensure security for population as well as staff and volunteers across the extended turbulent post-election period. 

The NS response plan has two elements: The first is the immediate response for the Nov 7th protest, called for by the opposition to be the largest protest experienced so far. For the immediate response, CVM aims to set up 42 first aid units across the country, activating the 1100 volunteers trained during their preparedness phase in the following locations (MAP). 

Participants in health coverage:
•	1100 volunteers - providing first aid
•	11 provincial secretaries
•	44 Technicians and drivers provinces 
•	06 technicians and drivers at the headquarters level  

The teams of volunteers will be supported and strengthened by the provincial delegations, through teams of provincial delegation staff (members and workers), for monitoring activities and technical support to volunteers.
Drivers – ensuring the movement of teams
Provincial staff – preparation of teams, allocation of material, monitoring communication with the vast team of volunteers, giving information to the headquarters and preparation of narrative and financial reports. 
Headquarters staff – preparation and submission of material to the provinces, interact with provincial teams, inform senior management and prepare reports.  

The second element is continuous response based on 3 potential scenarios defined in the humanitarian scenario analysis (see other attached document related to response). In summary, this response DREF will focus only on scenario 2 based on it's likelihood:
 
Scenario 2: Protest continue through the end of the year intermittently, with medium to significant number of injuries, but no further escalation. 
Key activity: Volunteers remain on stand by to respond with first aid services with their 42 first aid units (including ambulances), equipped to be able to respond to between 7-10 more protests that can take place across the remainder 2 months of the year. Continuous monitoring of situation for further escalation or de-escalation moments. Monitoring in communities. Continued socialization of RC role and promotion of peace-keeping, internal business continuity planning to ensure operational continuity. The scale up will cover: first aid unit items including 42 gazebos, water and cups for the units, and blankets. Additional first aid kits will be provided by Belgian RC contribution. The scale up will also support with enhanced safe access messaging for volunteers with dissemination of the role of RCRC movement. Scale up also covers further monitoring and security assessments, as well as development of key SOPs for NS to be able to continue to operate under this and similar events. 

Based on the likelihood of these scenarios, the Response DREF Operation, scaled-up from the prepardness DREF, will support NS in the implementation of activities under scenario 2. Together, the preparedness & response plan deploys trains volunteers in matters of First Aid, Safer Access and CEA to provide first aid services to those who have suffered a sudden injury or illness (including dehydration), aimed at stabilizing their condition until it is possible to obtain specialized medical assistance before, during, and in the period after elections. This includes engaging with community stakeholders to promote peace-keeping and clarify the role of the RC during elections. This allows volunteers and staff to provide health coverage in accordance with the principles of the movement and engage the community to promote peace-keeping (Humanity, Impartiality, Neutrality, Independence, Volunteering, Unity and Universality).
people_assisted: 55 districts across 11 provinces have been selected covering 36% of the entire country focusing on 5 districts in each province. Volunteers will be on stand-by and active through campigning period, voting day, and post election period.  Some volunteers may continue to be involved and some will be on stand-by (as protests may only occur in some areas more than others). Based on 1100 volunteers organized across 42 first aid units, each unit being able to assist 40 people a day on average across 16 different occasions (multiple days of campaigning (3), voting (1), immediate post-elections day protests (4), Nov 7 protest (1) and extended demonstrations after Nov 7th protest (7) = capacity to attend 26,880 people. Note this is response capacity, and ideally fewer people will actually need to be assisted.
operation_objective: The overall objective of the operation is to respond to fist aid needs of 26,880 people across the electoral period (campaigning, voting, post-election) by supporting the training and equipping of 1100 volunteers to promote well-being and prevent harm.
pmer: The monitoring process will be implemented throughout the period of validity of this plan, thus seeking to ensure the information contained in the initial plan on the status of the situation, stage of implementation, operational or strategic changes that need to be made. IFRC will support through PMER expertise and follow up with each province, as well as through technical support visits given the rising complexity of the operation.
major_coordination_mechanism:
Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) is active. IFRC is present at this meeting. CVM participated in clusters FSL, shelter, protection - yet these are active for the drought and conflict and are not currently focused on electoral preparedness. However, the issues may arise and be discussed in these forums.

Internally: The flow of information will follow the lines of command structures according to the CVM's organizational chart. Thus, all information on volunteers and DCs must be sent to the Provincial Secretaries of the CVM and then to the Central Headquarters.

Communication with the press must be made by the presidents of the DCs, Provincial Secretaries and the Secretary-General of the CVM or persons appointed by him.

A strategy-level movement meeting and an operations meeting are held with all stakeholders involved in the response on a daily basis, with the possibility of adjustment in the next few days
event_description:
Following Mozambique's October 9, 2024, elections, the political landscape has devolved into a period of demonstrations, characterized by allegations of electoral irregularities and a growing protest movement. The situation escalated when two opposition figures were shot, which ignited calls for large-scale protests and a nationwide seven-day strike beginning October 31st. So far, security forces have responded to maintain order. During the demonstrations, reports indicate that numerous people have been injured and several have lost their lives. The demonstrations has disrupted services and paralyzed key areas, particularly in Maputo, Nampula, and other key areas.
 
Opposition leaders have framed the 7 day strike and march in honor of the Murder of the Mozambican people during elections. Demonstrations, which began as peaceful protests, have gradually turned confrontational. The opposition has called for unity within the security forces, increasing concerns about possible internal confrontations within police ranks. A potential escalation is anticipated if security personnel join protestors, which would challenge state authority and may lead to drastic measures, including a state of emergency. The 7-day strike culminated with people occupying Maputo on November 7, with an estimated 1 million people joining from across the provinces.

Joint statement regarding the electoral process have been given by political parties, and separately by foreign embassies. It remains uncertain if mediation efforts can prevent further escalation.  Additionally, internet, mobile, and social media networks have been suffering disruptions across the country, increasing fears that communication shutdowns are being put in place to avoid sharing of information.

Trigger: largest Nation-wide protests on Nov 7th. The protest on Nov 7th caused widespread disruptions with military and police presence across Maputo city. Road access was blocked in and out of Maputo city, majority of businesses remained closed, and communication lines (internet and mobile) remained inconsistent. The main border with South Africa is closed due to it being burned down by protestors. There was significant looting of shops and trucks as well. At the end of the day, opposition leader gave a speech indicating that further protests would come until there was a closure regarding the electoral process.

needs_identified.title: protection_gender_and_inclusion
needs_identified.description:
People displaced from their residences are compelled to remain in open spaces. In general, the disaster amplifies the vulnerability of already at-risk groups within the community. In these public areas, where people are bound to stay in close proximity, there is an immediate need to create gender-friendly spaces as well as child-friendly spaces. This includes providing psychosocial support (PSS) and raising awareness about the prevention of sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV), as well as promoting referral pathways among the population, particularly for children and women.

Furthermore, as a large number of households have been displaced and affected, special care and attention must be given to children, vulnerable women (pregnant and lactating), people with disabilities, those with chronic illnesses, and the elderly, considering their heightened vulnerability. There is an urgent need to ensure menstrual hygiene and dignity for women and children through the distribution of dignity hygiene kits.

needs_identified.title: multi_purpose_cash_grants
needs_identified.description: The flood has affected more than 10,000 families. Many houses were submerged, leaving residents without food, clothes, and other essential daily items. The displaced families are staying in rented houses which creates additional economic burden. These families are facing challenges in affording daily household needs including food. Therefore, there is an urgent need to support these households by providing multi-purpose cash assistance. Volunteers on the ground have reported functioning markets in the affected areas.

needs_identified.title: community_engagement_and_accountability
needs_identified.description:
When engaging with communities, it is critical to ensure that information is not only broadcasted within the communities, but that response teams also set aside time to listen to the needs and interests of affected populations, especially those who are most marginalized and least likely to have a public voice. A process must be established to ensure that information from communities is not only heard but also acted upon by providing various mechanisms to listen to and respond to those voices.

During a disaster, this approach emphasizes a participatory response mechanism, supporting the community in recognizing needs, identifying recipients, and planning implementation. Regular consultations with stakeholders and communities are necessary to identify their needs, establish the beneficiary selection process, and coordinate the distribution of relief materials. Key messages and beneficiary selection criteria of NRCS will be shared with the local government and communities and beneficiary selection process will be agreed upon accordingly. Additionally, sector-specific key messages will be contextualized so that communities can understand and act upon them through existing feedback mechanisms.

needs_identified.title: shelter_housing_and_settlements
needs_identified.description:
According to detailed assessment data of NRCS, more than 26,500 people (5,300 households) were affected by the recent flooding and landslides. Many affected families are living outside their homes due to the extensive damage to their houses. As of 5 November, a detailed assessment was conducted over the 6 districts and the analysis is ongoing. According to the district chapter, the level of impact on various service sectors, the major needs of the communities are emergency shelter items including (tarpaulin, blankets, and mattresses), as well as household items and clothing, especially for families whose homes are uninhabitable or were completely swept away by the flood. 

Transitional shelter is also essential for families whose houses have been fully destroyed, as it will provide safety, dignity, and protection, particularly for vulnerable family members, including children, pregnant and lactating women, people with disabilities, the elderly, and those with chronic illnesses, which the local government will support. The Government has allocated a budget to cover the overall need for transitional shelter by providing conditional cash to the affected families. Therefore, the revised DREF plan has removed activities, and the budget has been allocated for other necessary sectors. All other activities in this sector remain unchanged. 

While there are actors, including the government, providing shelter support, response in remote areas may be delayed due to washed- away infrastructure and intermittent communication. The NRCS can help fill this gap by rapidly mobilizing its volunteers in both urban and rural areas, ensuring that families in hard-to-reach regions receive timely assistance.

needs_identified.title: health
needs_identified.description:
With the rains and flooding leading to limited WASH facilities, there is an increased risk of communicable diseases, the majority of which are waterborne. In addition, based on historical data, dengue cases are likely to rise dramatically in September and October, as the lack of proper sanitation measures may create an optimal breeding ground for mosquitoes. There is a need for promotional activities in order to aware communities of preventive measures.  As of 28 October 2024, 28,212 cases have been reported in 76 districts out of which 12 people have been reported to lose their lives due to Dengue. (Ministry of Health and Population: edcd.gov.np)

At a time when communities are dealing with various issues, it is essential to ensure that they continue to prioritize their health, including mental health. Mental health and psychosocial well-being may not be prioritized immediately during a disaster like this but neglecting them can lead to long-term negative effects if not addressed. In addition to psychosocial support, people need health promotion activities addressing a wide range of health risks, including raising awareness to continue regular basic health services, such as child immunizations, antenatal care (ANC) visits, institutional delivery, and referral services, which are required for immediate operation.

Winter needs also need to be considered in the operation, as many childhood illnesses, such as seasonal flu and pneumonia, are more prevalent during winter. As a result, people suffering from hypertension, heart disease, and other similar non-communicable diseases will require additional healthcare during this season. NRCS community volunteers are needed for community-based surveillance (CBS) of diseases to monitor and promptly report any possible outbreaks and track diseases like seasonal flu.

needs_identified.title: water_sanitation_and_hygiene
needs_identified.description:
Based on the NRCS detail assessment, the flood and landslide have major impact on water facilities as sources of drinking water, pipelines and taps are completely washed away in severely affected municipalities of targeted districts. The entire population living in these areas lacks safe drinking water. However, the findings of detail assessment are being consolidated, concrete information will be available once the report is finalized. Additionally, many families lost their homes including toilets facilities making them prone to various preventable diseases.

The late September flooding in the Kathmandu Valley has affected populations residing near rivers, particularly in slum areas, making them susceptible to waterborne diseases. However, the water started to recede from third day of the incident and things started to normalize after a week of the flooding.

planned_interventions.description:
1. Provide multi-purpose cash support for immediate needs to 800 families whose houses were fully damaged (NPR 15,000/CHF 107 as per MEB for one month as agreed among all humanitarian actors).
2. Conduct monitoring and surveys such as PDM survey, as part of the MPC distribution process.
planned_interventions.progress_towards_outcome:
As of 30 October, a total of 525 families in the rural municipalities of Sunkoshi, Golanjor, and Bethanchowk, located in Sindhuli and Kavrepalanchok respectively, successfully received the multi-purpose cash (MPC) assistance. Out of 525 families, DREF supported MPC distribution to 115 families from Kavre. The remaining 410 households from Sindhuli received MPC support from other in country support, which includes American Red Cross, Swiss Red Cross, Danish Red Cross, British Red Cross, and Finnish Red Cross. The distribution is ongoing in the remaining districts. 

In collaboration with local government to ensure that all processes were aligned with governmental regulations and expectations, each eligible household would receive 15,000 NPR (as per MEB). Following this approval, the MPC assistance was provided either through bank transfers or cash in hand to the beneficiaries, with all distributions categorized as non-conditional cash grants, allowing families the flexibility to use the funds according to their most pressing needs.

Major Change:
As of 6 November 2024, the target households of DREF operation who receive MPC support has been revised from 800 to 1800 families. It was because the affected families are residing in rented houses or relatives' home. And the detailed assessment data showed that the affected population is much higher than the initial assessment. The initial IFRC-wide target was 2,000 which has been revised to 3,316.

NRCS is planning to start health promotion and ECV activities in mid-November and expects to complete by December 2024. 

During the past month, Danish Red Cross contributed MHPSS services through the NRCS’ volunteer's mobilization to affected population. As of 30 October 2024, MHPSS service had reached 2,010 people in Kavre and Sindhuli effectively addressing the immediate psychological needs of those people in need. A total of 40 trained volunteers and Psychological First Aider (PF Aider) were mobilized by NRCS NHQ to the field to deliver psychosocial support to individuals affected by the disaster, particularly those who lost family members, homes, and personal assets. Additionally, an orientation on Protection, Gender, and Inclusion (PGI) was conducted for the volunteers in both Kavre and Sindhuli, while a self-care session was provided to 30 volunteers in Sindhuli to enhance their capacity to support others.

Major Change: 
The total target has been revised from 15,000 to 9,000 people to be reached with IFRC DREF support and 15,000 people targeted to be reached from the IFRC-wide support from in-country members (American Red Cross, British Red Cross, Danish Red Cross, Finnish Red Cross and Swiss Red Cross) on health.

planned_interventions.progress_towards_outcome:
As of 6 November, 500 people have received dignified hygiene kits. There are 860 kits dispatched by NRCS in different districts. The distribution of dignified hygiene kits is still ongoing.

The is no progress in hygiene promotion activities because the District Chapter volunteers are focusing more on the lifesaving responses, NFI and MPC distribution. NRCS arranges to commence those health promotion and ECV activities in mid-November and expects to complete by December 2024.

The NRCS NHQ deployed NDRT/WRT to the affected districts to conduct quick orientation for district-level volunteers. All district chapters have been mobilizing these volunteers in the affected communities who are engaged in distributing hygiene kits, aqua tab from NRCS existing stock and also conducting hygiene promotion sessions. Detail report about people reached is yet to be received from NRCS District Chapters. 

In the past month, following the devastating floods and landslides caused by heavy rainfall, significant efforts have been made in the Sindhuli district to address WASH needs. A comprehensive feasibility survey was conducted to assess and estimate the costs for 34 drinking water supply systems across two municipalities with the support of NRCS engineer team. This assessment is crucial for planning effective interventions to restore safe drinking water access.

NRCS District Chapters have been closely working with the local municipalities to conduct necessary renovations of damaged water facilities.
