needs_identified.title: shelter_housing_and_settlements
needs_identified.description: According to SRCS data, flash flooding caused by El Niño has damaged approximately 1,737 houses in six districts of Somaliland and Puntland. The floods have had severe destructive impacts on shelter, housing, and settlements, leaving a great number of the affected people displaced. Hence people are forced to leave their homes sleeping on the ground with nothing but the clothes they are wearing. There is a need for immediate shelter intervention. SRCS will prioritize response by providing shelter NFI kits which include tarpaulins, sleeping mats, blankets, kitchen and plastic sheets provision of training to volunteers in flood-prone target locations on early warning messaging, give technical assistance on evacuation plan, and dissemination of early warning information about flooding events, impact/damages, and other important information to the communities.

needs_identified.title: health
needs_identified.description:
The impact of the flash flooding has brought significant and multifaceted health risks and needs for the people in the affected areas. The situation led to increased risk of waterborne diseases due to the contamination of water sources and the damage of sanitation facilities.

Available primary and secondary data’s show that people recently affected by the floods are at high risk of vector-borne and airborne diseases, such as dengue, malaria, diarrhoea, and cholera, due to exposure to harsh weather, poor hygiene, and stagnant and polluted waters that serve as breeding grounds for mosquitoes and other disease vectors. Additionally, the flooding has had a negative impact on their psychosocial well-being.

Hence, it is critical to provide primary health services, including psychosocial support, must be provided to flood-affected people using static and mobile health facilities, along with basic health promotion awareness. Rapid-Response Volunteer Teams need refresher training on epidemic preparedness and promoting health and hygiene practices in targeted communities to address these needs effectively.

needs_identified.title: water_sanitation_and_hygiene
needs_identified.description:
The rapid assessment carried by SRCS team found that flash floods happened in flood affected areas damaged water facilities, created a shortage of clean water, contaminated water sources, destroyed sanitation facilities, and increased the incidence of waterborne diseases and this led to a shortage of clean water and safe sanitation, increased exposure to disease-causing pathogens, and poor hygiene practices. In addition, it also aggravates the need for the MHM and WASH NFIs such jerrican soaps, buckets, water purification chemicals distributions.

It also aggravates the need for the MHM and WASH NFIs such jerrican, soaps, hygiene kits, dignity kits, buckets, water purification chemicals distributions, desludging or rehabilitation of latrines and environmental clean-up campaigns should be conducted particularly focusing on putting in place drainage facilities in areas where water stagnates and becomes a breeding ground for mosquitoes.

Given the urgent situation, critical areas with the greatest damage to water supply and latrines must be rehabilitated, WASH NFIs distributed to help people treat and store available water safely, and hygiene promotion sensitization carried out to prevent the spread of waterborne diseases.

needs_identified.title: livelihoods_and_basic_needs
needs_identified.description: The flash flooding is also linked to a socio-economic impact, affecting the livelihoods of communities who rely on agriculture, livestock, and fishing.

needs_identified.title: protection_gender_and_inclusion
needs_identified.description: Most of the people affected by the flash floods are women and children. Vulnerable groups are at risk of exploitation, psychosocial trauma, and sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV). As such, PGI will be streamlined throughout the intervention, ensuring that volunteers receive adequate briefings during the various refreshers. SRCS will ensure that protection issues are taken into account and that everyone feels protected despite age, gender, and disability status. The National Society will conduct awareness-raising and orientation sessions on protection for volunteers. For the inclusion of everyone, engagement with people in the settlement site will be done to ensure that all the assistance is distributed equitably and impartially. Gender roles will be considered when setting up distribution times and dates as well as in hygiene promotion activities. As part of the needs assessment and analysis, a gender and diversity analysis will be included in all sector responses including Shelter, Livelihoods, Health, and WASH, to understand how different groups have been affected, which will inform any revision of the operational strategy.

needs_identified.title: community_engagement_and_accountability
needs_identified.description:
During the disaster such as flash floods, access to information is a challenge for the most vulnerable people.  This makes communicating with impacted populations and receiving feedback more difficult. People need to have a way of receiving information about the support available, how to access humanitarian assistance, and how to stay safe and healthy. There will also need to be a way for people to share information about their needs and how they can best receive assistance to meet their needs. It is ideal to have a place where the community can give feedback on the support they receive and essential that they know how to report issues.

Following previous operation, a community committee will be formed to support community engagement as they are direct representatives from their own communities. The community can directly provide feedback to members, which are essential for continuous improvements of the programme implementation.

summary_of_change:
An imminent DREF was launched on 14 Oct based on forecast from ICPAC, an imminent DREF was launch to ensure SRCS readiness and capacity to conduct early actions aiming to prevent the communities shelter, life and assets. Triggers were set as:  
- SRCS actions under the imminent DREF focused in the Somaliland and Puntland to address the risk of floods that were likely to materialise with cumulative 7 days rains of beyond 80mm.
- Trigger for evacuation were specific for each region and above thresholds detailed per areas to be monitored through the 7-day predictions of ICPAC, or local/region information of rainfall.
ALERT systems composed of weekly rainfall forecasts were monitored through ICPAC information. 

The above triggers were met during the week of 24 Oct to 31 Oct IGAD-ICPAC where it was predicted heavy to very heavy rainfall in parts of Somaliland and Puntland (“Very heavy to extremely heavy rainfall expected in parts of central to southern Ethiopia, extending into northern Somalia as well as in northern and southern parts of Uganda”, “Heavy rainfall (more than 200mm) expected in parts of central to southern Ethiopia and north-western coastal Somalia”). These rains have culminated in the floods and impact reported under the scope and scale. 

Due to the severity of the flooding in Puntland and Somaliland, the number of flood-affected households, displaced households, and the impact of the flooding in most of the affected areas, the initial plan is revised to scale-up from imminent to response. This covers:
- An extension to 6 months. 
- Response intevention based on assessment conducted in 2 November 2023. Priority intervention to assist 25,000 people in Awdal, Bari, Mudug, Nugaal, Togdheer and Woqooyiand Galbeed.  
- intervention to This is because some activities require adequate time for procurement, implementation, and budget adjustments based on the actual needs of the affected people. 
This brought the total allocation revised at CHF 597,478 with a second allocation of CHF 446,516.
- Maintain the early warning in the the most vulnerable communities at risk to flooding based on mapping related to medium- and short-term forecasts, historical data in the regions in above regions.

Normally the DREF responses only provide an immediate needs assistance where the affected communities’ resilience take time to recover. In this case, the DREF response is followed by an imminent DREF, which is a continuation of the readiness activities. This means that the response is to a previously forecasted event, and all the necessary coordination, preparation, information dissemination, and other preparedness work has already been accomplished. Therefore, the national society will be well-positioned to respond to the flooding disaster happened in a more effective, organized, and coordinated way, using its established systems and volunteers. Additionally, coordination with other partners and stakeholders will continue, as the coordination system is already established.

selection_criteria:
To ensure that the most vulnerable people are reached in the flash flood response operation, the primary selection criteria is based on a combination of factors and considerations that prioritize those who need help the most, the severity of the impact, the existing vulnerabilities of certain groups, and the social dynamics between different groups in terms of protection. 

The intervention targets the most affected regions of Awdal, Sahil, and Sanaag regions of Somaliland, and Nugaal, Bari, and Mudug regions of Puntland. The following criteria are used to select households for assistance: 
- Families whose houses have been submerged/destroyed and displaced
- Families and individuals directly impacted by the flash floods are the primary focus. This includes those who have suffered damage to their homes, and loss of livelihoods.
- Specific vulnerabilities and common social marginalized groups: Women, children, women/child headed households, people living with disabilities, pregnant and lactating mothers, the elderly (over 65), and low-income households.
- Households moving to relatives' houses, where resources are already limited, and the hosting communities are taking another burden by hosting families.
- Families with people with disabilities. 
- Specific priority to migrants and IDPs
ifrc: IFRC will sustain the capacities of the National Society. Support from the IFRC’s Regional Office for Africa is sustained through the standing support from the IFRC technical staff, which includes long-term Project Coordinator and WASH delegates based in Somaliland and surge delegates mobilized to support the Hunger Response Operation (Health, FSL, Communications, PMER/IM). In addition, operational standing support from the Finance, Logistics, and Security are provided remotely and through visits, as needed.
risk_security_concern:
Somalia's security situation is unpredictable and volatile, with the militant group Al-Shabab maintaining control of territory in southern Somalia. Al-Shabab frequently attacks military outposts in rural areas and civilian targets in Mogadishu, including airports, hotels, police stations, and government buildings. The group also frequently detonates improvised explosive devices (IEDs) at major checkpoints in the city. The port of Bosaso is a high-value target for militants operating in Puntland.

In Somaliland, especially Hargeisa, the safety/security threat situation is considerably better than in South and Central Somalia. There is a latent threat of violent extremism, stemming from mainly radical groupings such as Al-Shabaab. The threat of violent extremism assessed as being lower in Somaliland than in other areas of the Republic of Somalia.

The overall security environment in Puntland remains relatively stable and unpredictable. Security incidents and threat information also remained unchanged in terms of frequency and severity from previous years. 

Major extremism challenges exist in Bari and Mudug Regions. Extremism is the most serious threat in Puntland. Uncontrolled open borders facilitate infiltration of external threats into Puntland territory as it shares a long border with the central regions of Somalia. Due to its wide-open borders and weak territorial borderline security, illegal arms flow freely, extremist’s elements infiltrate easily, and drug and human smugglers operate largely unnoticed in this part of Somalia.

To reduce the risk of RCRC personnel falling victim to conflict, crime, extremism, health and road hazards active risk mitigation measures must be adopted. Security orientation and briefing for all teams prior to deployment be undertaken to help ensure safety and security of response teams. Standard security protocols about general norms, cultural sensitivity and an overall code of conduct be put in place. Minimum-security requirements will be strictly maintained. All National Society and IFRC personnel actively involved in the operations must successfully complete prior to deployment the respective IFRC security e-learning courses (i.e., Level 1 Fundamentals, Level 2 Personal and Volunteer Security and Level 3 Security for Managers). IFRC security plans will apply to all IFRC staff throughout the operation. Area specific Security Risk Assessment will be conducted for any operational area should any IFRC personnel deploy there; risk mitigation measures will be identified and implemented.

Personnel must have insurance. Minimum security equipment required: Functional satellite phones, communication tools, advanced first aid kits, PEP kits, hibernation stocks, safe accommodation, and fully kitted vehicles. Movement should be undertaken after road assessments.

Some areas of Puntland and Somaliland are subject to travel restrictions, including Las Anod. All IFRC staff traveling in these areas must adhere to the established movement strategy and coordinate with the security officer covering Somalia and coordinating with NS and movement partners.
national_authorities:
Joint assessments conducted by the government and the SRCS Branches in October 2023 identified the following community needs: shelter, food, WASH, basic necessities, and health and hygiene. To date, the government regional offices and SRCS Branches have provided affected households with shelter and WASH NFI, including mattresses, blankets, sleeping mats, jerrycans, buckets, and water purification tablets.

To date, the government regional offices have started provided the affected households with Shelter and WASH NFI include mattresses, blankets, sleeping mats, jerrycans, buckets and water purification tablets. 

Coordination and Communication: The government has been actively coordinating with local authorities, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), NGOs and relief agencies to streamline relief efforts. Communication channels were established to disseminate information and instructions to the public about safety measures and available assistance led by NADFOR.

Evacuation and Shelter: Evacuation plans were put into action to move residents from high-risk areas to safer locations. Temporary shelters, such as community centres and schools, were set up to accommodate those displaced by the floods. The government requested the international partners to provide affected households with essential supplies like food, water, and blankets

The national authorities have called for a number of preparedness meetings with humanitarian organizations in the country. Humanitarian organizations were requested to advocate anticipatory actions that will prevent loss of life and property. 

The national authorities suggest a very short window only for few weeks to be ready and mitigate the impact of El Nino, by taking early and well-informed actions.

partner_national_society: Country partners, including the Finnish, German, Norwegian, Canadian, Icelandic, and Danish Red Cross, have active programs in Somaliland and have been supporting the SRCS in health, disaster risk management, livelihoods, resilience, emergency, and hunger crisis response.
event_scope:
Assessment reports from 2 Nov indicate flash floods caused by heavy rains and strong winds have affected at least 17,529 people in Somaliland and Puntland, killing 4 (1 in Berbera, 1 in Eyl and 2 in Bander- Beyla districts) and injuring 12. Assessments are still under way and the numbers are expected to rise as more rains are forecast by IGAD-ICPAC. 
The floods result from continued intense rainfall events recorded across parts of Somaliland and Puntland. Since early October, the rainfall predictions have varied from less than 50 to 200 mm from mid October to week 1 of November. These floods and heavy rains have caused widespread damage and disrupted communities in the affected regions, damaging or destroying houses, water points, livestock, health facilities, schools, hospitals, mosques, small businesses, and transportation. Stagnant water in key areas, such as markets, health facilities, schools, and communal centres, has exacerbated the hardship and displacement.

The floods are reported to have damaged or destroyed over 1,097 houses, 120 semi-permanent houses, 520 IDP shelters, 46 business shops/centres, latrines, water facilities, and crops on at least 60 farms. The roofs of two primary schools, two mosques, and a hospital have also been blown off and vehicles swept away. In addition, 33 goats and sheep have been killed. The floods have also damaged some infrastructure and disrupted the supply chain for essential goods and services, making it difficult for people to access food, water, healthcare, and education.

The floods have significantly impacted the physical and mental well-being of affected populations, many of whom are already living in poverty and facing food insecurity. Many people have lost their homes, essential services, and accessibility due to flooding. Residential houses and makeshift shelters for displaced people have been inundated, and many people are still unable to access their homes due to stagnant water. This increases the risk of water- and vector-borne diseases, mental health problems, and exacerbates existing vulnerabilities.

Furthermore, the flash flooding is also linked to a socio-economic impact, affecting the livelihoods of communities who rely on agriculture, livestock, and fishing. Vulnerable groups, including women, children, the elderly, and persons with disabilities, face increased risks, while protection concerns, such as gender-based violence and child protection issues, have emerged as critical challenges.

This is particularly concerning as many people as possible in the area are already living in poverty and have not yet recovered from the impacts of a prolonged 4-year drought. The floods have made these challenges even worse and have increased the risk of displacement and conflict. Hence it is important to scale up the Imminent DREF into response DREF to prevent or limit any of the flood impact as minimum as possible since the amount of rain received in some parts of the areas is beyond 80mm which caused significant damages on the community and led some of them to evacuate to safe locations.

In first half of October, 50 mm and 100 mm in northern parts of Burco district in Togdheer region, Ceel Afwyene and Ceerigaabo districts in Sanaag region, and Bosasso district in Bari region; heavy rainfall of between 150 mm and 200 mm in southern parts of Togdheer region, and Las Anod;  50 mm and 100 mm over several areas in Togdheer and Sool regions, Hargeisa district in Woqooyi Galbeed region, Ceel Afweyn district and southern parts of Ceerigaabo district in Sanaag region, Burtinle district in Nugaal region, and isolated areas in Bari region. Further to the above the ICPAC weather forecast from October 31 to November 7, 2023, predicts continued heavy and extremely heavy rainfall in most areas of Awdal, Sahil, and Sanaag regions of Somaliland, as well as some coastal areas of Bari, Nugaal, and Mudug regions of Puntland. This necessitates a scaled-up response to provide humanitarian assistance, including food, water, shelter, and healthcare, to flood-affected populations and also to support long-term recovery and rehabilitation.

Somaliland and Puntland experiences recurrent floods, which are becoming more frequent and severe due to climate change. These floods cause enormous damage to infrastructure, lives, and livelihoods, especially among the most vulnerable people. Several factors exacerbate the risks and consequences of floods in these countries, including unregulated occupation of flood-prone areas (riverbeds), poverty, recurring climatic shocks and conflicts, the state's limited economic capacity to intervene and support flood victims, and the absence of a sustainable flood prevention policy. 
The next week forecast also raised concerned with additional rainfall likely from 100mm in some of the already affected areas.

The United Nations and other actors have been actively engaged in addressing the El-Nino event and through the existing coordination platforms, a consensus has been reached, leading to the development of a cluster level comprehensive contingency plans.

Under this plan, each cluster had to submit its own contingency plan by Sep 26/2023, outlining specific actions and measures to mitigate the impact of El-Nino. The collective efforts of all partners involved aim to ensure a coordinated and effective response. Concerning the contingency plans: 
•  All clusters leads have to share their respective cluster contingency plans based on what they have and the gaps (Disaster Agency / OCHA template). 
•  Disaster Agency / OCHA have to share a template that is used by cluster leads for their submissions. 
•  Clusters have to participate in El Nino Preparedness/contingency planning meetings.
response_strategy:
Imminent 
As part of anticipatory actions an imminent DREF was launched on 14 Oct to with the aims to mitigate the impact of the forecasted El Niño, which is likely to bring floods, flash floods and landslides. The intervention will target over 25,000 people in the the most vulnerable communities at risk to flooding based on mapping related to medium- and short-term forecasts, historical data in the regions of Awdal, Bari, Mudug, Nugaal, Togdheer and Woqooyiand Galbeed. 

The intervention prioritized the actions to mitigate the immediate risk on life, the exposition to further losses and 
health risk for already vulnerable communities and complex humanitarian situation that could worsen the health, 
livelihood and shelter situation with enhanced floods following El Nino phenomenon predicted to affect the country 
until December. In that sense, the plan implemented since the launch included so far:
1. Branches Readiness: refresher briefings on shelter, DRR, WASH and health focusing on flood risk reduction and community early warning activities, assessment, risk messages, mobilization of staff, volunteers and NDRTs
2. Community level preparedness: branches monitored situation and supported early warning systems, support local government in the preparation of pre-identified evacuation centers/areas, engaged local partners and existing social network for risk communication to most vulnerable groups. Mobilization of region key social communication networks, including radio, printing and distributions of IEC material's.  
3. Stocks: started stock acquisition, pre positioning, checked FSP agreements. 
4. Early actions for risk reduction focused on: activated community early warning procedures and supported evacuation of people at risk.   
5. Coordination: the coordination with local govt and partners on rapid/multi sector assessments, etc., gaps analysis.    

Response 
Based on assessment conducted on 2 November 2023 after successive floods broke out in Puntland and Somaliland, Somalia RC is adding to the early actions supported a response intervention for thousands of people affected already by the floods as per the predictions.
The response aims to meet the direct needs of the most vulnerable flood-affected people for as follows:
- Emergency shelter and essential household items: through distribution of shelter NFIs (tarpaulins, rope, mattresses, blankets, sleeping mats, kitchen sets, and mosquito nets).
- Access to livelihood and basic needs through a provision of multipurpose cash grants or assistance. The amount is aligned with the Cash working group recommendations. Cash transfer will be a one-off transaction. It is anticipated that one month will allow the situation to stabilize, and people could return to their homes. The transfer value will cover 80% of the minimum expenditure basket (MEB). Therefore, this MEB covers the basic needs of a family of 6 members, such as food, water, hygiene items, communication costs. Market assessment and needs assessment will provide further insight into the relevance of the transfer value and the need to adjust to cover inflation and some items not included, such as the kitchen set. While the coverage of telecommunication of Telesom and Golis, the two service providers of SRCS is good, and most households own a phone. 
- Health: Through support to existing mobile health clinics, provision of first aid, health promotion activities, psychosocial support (MHPSS), and reinforcing capacity of volunteers on epidemic control.
- WASH: Through rehabilitation of water infrastructure and sanitation facilities, and distribution of essential MHM dignity kits and WASH NFIs (jerricans, soaps, buckets, water purification chemicals/aqua tabs, and others), and provide hygiene promotion. In addition, desludging or rehabilitation of latrines and environmental clean-up campaigns particularly focusing on putting in place drainage facilities in areas where water stagnates and becomes a breeding ground for mosquitoes.
- PGI and CEA: Through training and mobilization of volunteers but also promotions and integration to sectoral priority approach
- Coordination: Implement an effective coordination system to avoid duplication of assistance with other stakeholders. This response will be conducted as a complementarity approach both with internal projects and interventions of other actors. The coordination system will include a mechanism for sharing information between the different SRCS projects, mainly on targeting and relevant approaches and gaps in the distributions conducted. 

To address the need of collecting more information on needs and updated gaps, as the situation continues to evolve, through this DREF operation, SRCS, supported by IFRC/PNS, will perform a multi-sectoral assessment to ascertain the precise needs of flood affected people in Awdal, Sahil, and Sanaag regions of Somaliland, and Nugaal, Bari, and Mudug regions of Puntland. The assessment report will aim to update on priorities for possible additional support. Especially with considerations of evolution of the humanitarian situation and stakeholders’ intervention.  The planned assessment aims also to ensure information are cross-checked and real time update are done and considered on other partners assistance and changes in priorities in any case. 

During the imminent  phase a comprehensive mapping of NFIs was carried out in coordination with all partners.   The DREF response is complemented by other Movement support such as the ICRC provision of assorted Shelter and WASH NFIs for 1,400 households to support flood affected people in Puntland. In addition, the response will replenish the NFIs provided as DP stock through the PP and Red Ready. Danish Red Cross will also provide funds to the NS which on confirmation will be coordinated as part of the overall NS response plan along with this DREF.
people_assisted:
Imminent 
The imminent DREF targeted at least 25,000 people considered to be at most risk to floods and flash floods based on risk mapping and forecasts for Somaliland and Puntland. 

Response target: 6 Regions - 3 in Somaliland (Awdal, Sahil, and Sanaag) and 3 in Puntland (Nugaal, Bari, and Mudug)
Based on the assessment and gaps in the response the DREF will target 1,100 households (6,600 people) prioritizing those whose houses were submerged/destroyed and not receiving support. The response will prioritize the most vulnerable including IDPs.
operation_objective:
The overall objective of this DREF is to scale-up the Somalia RC actions in this floods season from anticipatory actions to a response intervention following the cumulative impact of floods assessed on 2nd November. After the early actions engaged in Awdal, Bari, Mudug, Nugaal, Togdheer and Woqooyiand Galbeed; the NS is keeping the early warning while engaging resources to support 6,600 households directly affected / displaced by flash flooding in 6 Regions - 3 in Somaliland (Awdal, Sahil, and Sanaag) and 3 in Puntland (Nugaal, Bari, and Mudug). 

The operation will be for six months providing comprehensive humanitarian assistance, including shelter, health, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH), and cash voucher assistance, while mainstreaming protection, gender and inclusion (PGI), and community engagement and accountability (CEA).
pmer:
•  The Operations team and NS leadership will oversee all operational, implementation, monitoring and evaluation, and reporting aspects of the DREF implementation. 
•  The Operations team will also work closely with IFRC Nairobi Cluster Delegation office and will be responsible for performance-based management systems and the overall quality. 
•  DREF progress monthly reports will be compiled by the National Society, informing the IFRC on the progress and challenges of the operation, along with a monitoring plan/indicator tracking table to map out, ensure the collection, and keep track of the key indicators.

major_coordination_mechanism:
To ensure timely action and preparedness, Government, UN and other Actors are actively working together to develop a comprehensive plan. By pooling resources, expertise and knowledge, the aim is to minimize the potential impact of this event in the communities. The collective focus is on implementing a robust preparedness and response plan that encompasses various sectors.
 
In Somaliland, NADFOR, supported by UNOCHA, plans to establish a regular coordination mechanism in response to this crisis. A coordination meeting will be held on an ad-hoc basis.
 
In Puntland all cluster leads are to share their respective cluster contingency plans based on what they have and the gaps (MoHADM/OCHA template).  
 
Line ministers of Somaliland aside from UNOCHA will be coordinated to ensure accurate targeting and avoid duplication.

The various clusters are active; NS and movement partners are part of them for information sharing on different sectoral approaches.

NS will take part on the coordination with UN and has already engaged some actions under this complementary system. NS coordinates locally with UN counterparts, especially in Somaliland on health, for example with UNICEF funding mobile health clinics and nutrition projects. Both Somaliland and Puntland coordinate and support cluster/TWG joint assessments, etc.
event_description:
Since September 22, 2023, El Niño-induced heavy rains and strong winds have caused flash floods and heavy rainfalls in Somaliland's Awdal (Garbo-Dader district), Sahil (Berbera district), and Sanaag (Erigavo districts) regions, and Puntland's Nugaal (Eyl district), Bari (Banderbeyla district, Galkayo district), and Mudug (Galkayo district) regions, severely impacting people's lives and movement. 

Continued rains particularly since mid Oct have resulted in flash floods in the six regions listed above - by 2 Nov the NS had reports of several communities being affected with more than 20,000 people reported affected in the northern regions. The flooding situation gives concrete form to the forecasts and analysis made in the DREF framework of proactive actions launched in October to prevent/mitigate the impact.

Indeed, since quarter 3, ICPAC meteorological forecasts predicted a probability of 10 days of above-average rainfall (exceeding 100 to 300 mm.) 65 to 85% of above-average rainfall in central and southern Somalia and 65 to 55% in the North zone. The study of flooding thresholds over the last 5 years during the same seasons has also helped to confirm the likelihood of an impact usually observed between 80mm and 150mm in the projected period of peak flooding following ICPAC (last week of September to 24 October). Considering the negative effect of El Nino on the Deyr rainy season, the impact analysis demonstrated the likelihood of heavy flooding in the region. See the DREF plan for the full analysis and sources.  

The Somali Red Crescent committed to limiting/prevent the impact of this potential impact on communities in the North zone, taking into account security factors, intervention possibilities in other regions in the South and coordination in the country. SRCS had started to respond to the needs while keeping the early warning in the alert areas.

needs_identified.title: health
needs_identified.description: The migrants stranded at the borders are found to suffer different health issues including injuries, chronic illnesses, first-degree sunburns in the summer and expected hypothermia in the winter. Many injuries have not been dealt with quickly due to the distance or the lack of knowledge of migrants of first aid, and there is a clear need for psychological support services, especially for women and children. The area at the border lacks basic health care services and IOM has secured the provision of basic health services in the center. A need for Psycho-Social Support is needed especially with the presence of a high number of pregnant women and a significant number of children. A risk of TB is also high few cases are identified in the center of Al-assa.

needs_identified.title: water_sanitation_and_hygiene
needs_identified.description:
There's a severe need for drinking water and hygiene kits to cover the needs of the migrants at the border and at the shelters. In fact, the detention centers are suffering from over-crowdedness with a high risk of communicable and non-communicable diseases. Therefore, ensuring hygiene security in the shelter is essential.
The centers have WASH facilities but they need rehabilitation which the national society will seek to cover through the support of different funding.

needs_identified.title: migration_and_displacement
needs_identified.description: As the migrants have been left at the borders with no means of communicating with their families, there's a need to facilitate their access to phones to contact their families and the embassies of their countries which is secured through the support of ICRC.

needs_identified.title: shelter_housing_and_settlements
needs_identified.description:
The migrants are found in open areas in very difficult weather conditions. The authorities have provided shelter in mainly Al-Assa detention center. However, with the limited relief items available from the government and the winter approaching, winterization items (especially thermal blankets) are needed. 
As the health risks are high, cleaning kits are also important to maintain minimum hygienic conditions within the centers which are suffering from limited space and an increasing number of migrants.

needs_identified.title: livelihoods_and_basic_needs
needs_identified.description:
Migrants at the border are left with no means of survival, no food or water. There's a clear need for ready food parcels and dry food parcels to cover the immediate needs and the needs of the migrants during their stay in the shelters until they return to their home countries. Given the temperature drop especially that the migration route is across the desert, dry high-caloric food items are needed for immediate response.
The national society provided the rescued migrants with small individual emergency food packages and will continue providing the affected population in the shelter with dry food as the shelters have kitchens.
As IOM is providing weekly medical check ups for the migrants, the basic health services are secured for the population in need.

summary_of_change:
The National Society has been going through structural changes that affected all the programmes implementation. In fact, the Secretary General of LRCS was changed twice within less than two months – 28/08/2023 and 24/10/2023-. Hence, implementation of the activities according to the timeline faced challenges as such changes imply technical focal points turnover and discontinuation of processes. Additionally, on Sunday, September 10 -few weeks after the approval of the DREF-, storm Daniel hit Libya’s north-eastern part of the country causing one of biggest catastrophes in the modern history of the country with 10,000 dead. All the resources and the personnel of the National Society has been diverted to the response to the Derna Crisis for over two months. Therefore, the response to the migration crisis at the Libyan-Tunisian borders was minimized.
The overall budget has not changed. However, some activities funds were reallocated in order to ensure efficiency and effectiveness of the resources use in light of the Daniel Storm floods response. In fact, the capacity building funds were reallocated to the procurement for a longer sustainable response to the influx of migrants with the second influx wave.

event_scope:
Since the second week of July, Libyan border guards have been coming to the rescue of sub-Saharan migrants expelled by the Tunisian authorities at the Libyan-Tunisian borders. 
According to the Libyan authorities, the migrants were found abandoned without water, food, or shelter in temperatures exceeding 50 degrees in an uninhabited area close to Al-Assah, which is about 15 kilometers (15 miles) inside Libyan territory and 150 kilometers (93 miles) west of Tripoli.
The Libyan government issued a statement on Tuesday 25 July announcing the discovery of five bodies of migrants who died in the desert in an area on the border with Tunisia.
Libya have become home to at least 600,000 sub-Saharan migrants. The numbers are increasing and the duration of the migrants' stay is prolonged until the voluntary return program is prepared with the International Organization for Migration.
Rescued migrants have been found to suffer from physical injuries such as first-degree burns due to the heatwaves hitting the area and were in very critical conditions, health services and personal hygiene materials were provided, and it is expected to receive an additional number of immigrants during the current week. 
Local authorities contacted the Libyan Red Crescent to reach out for help as the number of migrants has exceeded the shelters capacities. The National Society responded to the humanitarian needs immediately and assisted the affected people by providing first aid services, drinking water and snacks, and migrants were hosted by the local authorities inside the shelter.
Due to the absence of embassies for some nationalities, their deportation will be delayed in the long term and their presence will remain until intervention is made by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the International Organization for Migration.
The situation continues to develop and the humanitarian situation continuous to deteriorate with more people arriving at the Tunisian-Libyan borders in addition to the heatwaves experienced during this period. Different sources reported that several bodies were recovered from the area. LRC is the only entity responding in the field.
During the second week of October 2023, a second wave of influx of migrants has arrived at the Tunisian-Libyan borders and they were detained by the Libyan government while waiting for sustainable solutions. Consequently, the Detention Center of Al-Assa is currently hosting around 1200 migrants ( 1090 men, 55 women, 40 children, 15 babies). According to the rapid needs assessment by LRCS, there are two identified cases of Tuberculosis which due to the poor hygienic conditions could lead to an outbreak of TB in the center. Additionally, there are 5 pregnant women in different stages of pregnancy. Children are suffering from the lack of appropriate food and clothing. Therefore, the needs for support to migrants in the Tunisian-Libyan borders are even higher at the moment and the response gaps are significant.

event_description:
On July 14th, the Libyan Red Crescent was informed by the local authorities that 1,100 migrants had been detected on the Libyan-Tunisian borders. The authorities requested the LRC to respond to the event. These migrants, originating from different African countries, were passing through Tunisia in an attempt to cross to Europe and have been held by the Tunisian authorities and expelled at the Tunisian borders with other countries including Libya. The migrants had crossed the Tunisian territory and were hosted by the Libyan border guard forces.
The Libyan Red Crescent continued to provide support and humanitarian aid for over a month until both governments reached an agreement where the Tunisian government agreed to take the responsibility of 126 migrants (76 men, 42 women, 8 children) in mid-August. 
The rest of the migrants were being managed by the Libyan authorities which intercepts them and detains them mainly in Al-Assa detention center. Both government agreed that each will be responsible for the migrants intercepted on its respective territory. Libya has witnessed an influx of around 1200 migrants in the second week of October and it is expected to have a continuous influx from Tunisia in the next months.

national_society_actions.title: assessment

national_society_actions.description:
The national authorities have set up evacuation plans in local schools to accommodate those displaced from their homes.
The Algeria Red Crescent ARC has distributed 100 tents to serve as a temporary shelter for those who reside in remote areas with no nearby shelters. The national society also distributed 2,000 mattresses and 1,996 blankets to the affected families.

national_society_actions.title: water_sanitation_and_hygiene
national_society_actions.description: The ARC has distributed 3,750 Hygiene kits to the families in the temporary shelters, in addition to 100,000 bottles of water, and has deployed 2 Water tanks with a capacity of 1,000L each to provide the affected people with clean drinking water.

needs_identified.title: livelihoods_and_basic_needs
needs_identified.description: The majority of affected people live off crops and livestock that were affected by the wildfires (9 chicken coops with the capacity of 1000 chicken each, 22 lambs, and 35 family-owned agricultural lands were reported to have burned down in Jijel based on initial assessments)

needs_identified.title: shelter_housing_and_settlements
needs_identified.description: A large number of people were forced to leave their houses (170 families by the second day in Jijel, Bouira and Bejaia) due to the fires and the number of tents in stock is very limited compared to the gravity of the disaster, and the schools prepared as shelters are getting filled quickly. At the time of submitting this request, 3,880 people are very sheltered in the temporary shelters provided by the national authorities, while others are either staying in tents provided by the national society or have relocated to stay with relatives. These people have lost their shelters and their shelter items and are in need of basic household items such as mattresses and blankets among other needs.

needs_identified.title: water_sanitation_and_hygiene
needs_identified.description: the fires have caused infrastructure damage to water  and sewage system networks. Rehabilitation of these networks will be carried out by the national authorities. Immediate need for drinking water and WASH facilities remain urgent needs for the people who lost their households to the fires. Due to the nature of temporary shelters, it is expected that some hygiene and health issues may arise due to crowdedness.

needs_identified.title: health
needs_identified.description:
The immediate risk to life and physical health: injuries (severe burn injuries), respiratory issues including asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and casualties, leading to an increased demand for emergency medical services.
Many affected people experience post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD),  anxiety,  depression,  and other mental health issues.
Overwhelmed healthcare facilities and disruption of health services, as well as strain on medical supplies and resources (shortages in essential items).
The displacement of people and overcrowded living conditions in temporary shelters can facilitate the spread of infectious diseases. These needs will not be addressed under this operation but will be covered by the national authorities with the support of the national society.

indicators.title: # of food parcels distributed

planned_interventions.description: • Distribute food parcels for 3,900 families for 3 months
planned_interventions.progress_towards_outcome:
The national society distributed 11,698 food parcels to 3,900 families during this operation from its stock. The procurement of the parcels to replenish the national society's stock is ongoing. In response to logistical challenges and constraints in the supply chain, modifications have been made to the contents of these essential food provisions.
Specifically, changes have been implemented in the composition of the food parcels, necessitating a substitution strategy. The ARC has opted to replace items like beans and lentils with more readily available alternatives which are pasta and rice. This decision was made in light of the temporary unavailability of the former items, ensuring that recipients continue to receive sustenance despite the supply chain limitations.
This modification underscores the adaptability and responsiveness of relief efforts in the face of logistical hurdles. By swiftly adjusting the contents of the food parcels, the ARC remains committed to providing essential nutritional support to those in need, even amidst challenges in sourcing specific food items.
The primary goal remains unchanged: to ensure that the food parcels cater to the nutritional requirements of beneficiaries. This shift in content is a strategic maneuver to ensure the uninterrupted provision of vital sustenance to affected communities, reflecting the ARC's commitment to adaptability and resilience in fulfilling their humanitarian mandate.

summary_of_change:
A one-month extension to the timeframe of the operation is requested to ensure comprehensive reporting and the successful culmination of the operation.
Moreover, alterations are being implemented in the operational strategy, particularly concerning the procurement of some items. This includes modifications to the composition of food parcels and hygiene kits aiming to better meet the needs of the intended recipients. Furthermore, there was an increase in the quantity of distributed water intended for the affected population.
To fortify and streamline operations, an operations manager was deployed for a four-month period, bringing expertise in Project Management, Evaluation, and Reporting (PMER). Additionally, this manager conducted a pivotal Disaster Relief Emergency Fund (DREF) training session, upskilling 20 individuals within the organization.
Notably, the IFRC was approached to authorize two crucial procurement changes aimed at providing essential assistance to those in need and replenishing depleted stocks. This involved strategic alterations in the composition of food parcels, substituting beans and lentils with pasta and rice due to the unavailability of the former product.
Simultaneously, modifications were sought for hygiene kits, expanding their contents from shampoo, shower gel, and towels to include an array of additional hygiene products. Furthermore, there's been a deliberate increase in the quantity of distributed water intended for the affected population.
Recognizing the urgency of acquiring necessary responses and completing essential reporting, an extension of the operational timeframe by an additional month was formally requested. This extension is crucial for timely resolution from the IFRC and to ensure the successful conclusion of the ongoing operation. These collective efforts underscore the commitment to swift, comprehensive, and effective action in alleviating the plight of the impacted communities.

The requested changes seek to enhance the effectiveness and comprehensiveness of the ongoing relief efforts, addressing various aspects of the community's needs, and shall not require an increase to the original allocated budget.
icrc: ICRC are present in the country and are supporting the structure of the national society but have no direct role in supporting this response.
selection_criteria:
The operation will attempt to target all of the population affected by the fires, taking into consideration the prioritization of the people most in need including:
-	Families who have their households completely or partially damaged by the fires. 
-	Families who have lost their livelihoods and are in need for immediate food and water support
-	Female headed households
-	Families with people with disabilities, elderly people and injured people due to the fires.
ifrc: The IFRC has been supporting in the monitoring and assessment of the situation including daily risk watch of the heatwave, providing technical support in the completion of relevant reports and documentation as well as designing the intervention and setting the budget.
national_authorities:
The Algerian Government deployed around 12 aircrafts, and 6 water bombers to control the fires, in addition to the participation of 8,000 civil defense personnel, 529 vehicles, and 10 military convoys from other regions in the country.
The government also participated in the evacuation and rescue of  1,500 people who were stranded by the fires.
The national authorities requested the Algerian Red Crescent Society to participate in the
response to this event and continue to coordinate with the national society on the response operation.
surge_personnel_deployed: Deployment of an operations manager to support the implementation of this operation was agreed upon with the national society.
partner_national_society: The Spanish Red Cross is present in the country but is not involved in the operation.
event_scope:
Algeria has been exposed to heat waves for over 60 days, with extreme weather patterns with temperatures exceeding 45°C in June and 50°C in July. The country was expected to witness local fires because of the weather conditions and the severe summer season. Additional factors have turned local fires into uncontrollable wildfires in the 3rd week of July.
The wildfires have reached several wilayas of the northeast, the most affected being: Bejaïa, Skikda, Tizi ouzou, Bouira, Jijel, Boumerdes. A total of 30,000 people were affected by the wildfires. So far, at least 34 deaths have been registered by the Algerian government and more than 700 people have been injured.
Homes, livestock, and crops were heavily affected, which directly impacted the well-being of the population, elderly people, and children. The national society was one of the first responders to the event, deploying its teams to conduct assessments of the magnitude of the effects of this event.
A total of 3,880 people were provided shelter in the evacuation centers while the rest of the people were provided with tents by the national society or decided to relocate to stay with relatives. The fires had a significant impact on the livelihoods of the impacted population.
human_resource: 20 staff from the national society in different capacities are involved in this operation with one project coordinator assigned by the national society as the focal point in addition to 500 volunteers.
title: Algeria Fire 2023
logistic_capacity_of_ns: Sourcing of relief items /Food Packages is to be primarily done locally with the option of international procurement is needed in consultation and support from GHS & SCM Unit. The purchase of food items is to be done primarily from the local market, with adequate certification process (independent inspection / Lab testing to be carried out. Technical approvals to be sought/received from IFRC through the support of IFRC MENA, Supply Chain Management Unit (IFRC GHS&SCM MENA) in Beirut. Any additional logistics support can be made available by the IFRC GHS&SCM MENA, as need.
un_or_other_actor: N/A
response_strategy:
To achieve the objective of the operation, the national society will provide 3,900 families (19,500 people) with food parcels, and 3,750 families with WASH services including water and hygiene kits to cover their needs for 3 months. In addition to replenishing 2,000 mattresses, and 2,000 blankets that were distributed to the families that lost their households to the fires. The national authorities are currently working on addressing the long term needs of the affected population. In the meantime, the national society plans to provide 50 tents as a temporary shelter to the families who lost their homes to the fires and were residing in remote areas that do not have official shelters prepared by the authorities.
The IFRC received a request from the NS to authorize pivotal adjustments in procurement procedures, aiming at effectively aiding those in dire need and restocking essential supplies. These modifications encompassed two crucial areas of assistance provision.
 
Initially, alterations were enacted in the composition of food parcels, strategically substituting beans and lentils with pasta and rice due to the unavailability of the former items in the market. This proactive adjustment ensured the continued provision of sustenance to beneficiaries despite logistical challenges in sourcing specific food items.
Simultaneously, there was a concerted effort to refine the contents of hygiene kits. The initial components, encompassing shampoo, shower gel, and towels, were broadened to include a more comprehensive array of additional hygiene products. This expansion aimed to enhance personal hygiene practices among recipients and better equip them to combat health risks prevalent in their circumstances.
Furthermore, a deliberate escalation in the quantity of distributed water to the affected population was initiated, acknowledging the critical importance of access to clean water in mitigating various health challenges faced by the community.
In light of these multifaceted adjustments and the urgency to acquire necessary responses, a formal request was made to extend the
operational timeframe by an extra month. This extension was deemed imperative to facilitate timely responses from the IFRC, complete the required reporting, and ensure the successful closure of the ongoing operation.
people_assisted: This operation targets the population affected by the wildfires in the mentioned most affected 6 wilayas (Bejaia, Bouira, Tizi Ouzou, Jijel, Skikda, Boumerdes). With a focus on families whose households were completely destroyed and are either currently residing in the shelters prepared by the authorities or in tents provided by the national society until they are relocated to permanent shelters.
operation_objective: The DREF operation aims to meet the immediate needs and to support 19,500 people affected by the wildfires in Bejaia, Bouira, Tizi Ouzou, Jijel, Skikda, Boumerdes, through the provision of Household items, Water and hygiene kits and food parcels.
pmer:
In direct coordination with the PMER and Quality assurance unit at IFRC MENA RO, a monitoring plan will be developed and implemented during this response. The PMER and Quality assurance unit comprises PMER, IM and CEA capacities that will be directly coordinating with ARC. The support will cover planning, monitoring, data collection and analysis along with CEA activities whenever needed. 
Biweekly meetings will also be organized between the operations team at IFRC MENA RO with the national society and IFRC surge team to follow up on the operation to ensure smooth implementation and address challenges as they come up.
event_description:
Around 35 wildfires have been rapidly spreading across the northeastern region of Algeria in more than 11 regions since July 24th causing extensive devastation. The disaster has had a profound impact on 6,000 families, with the Algerian Government reporting 34 confirmed deaths. The affected population heavily relies on crops and livestock, both of which have been severely impacted by the wildfires, resulting in further hardships for the communities. Many homes have been reduced to ashes, leaving families displaced and vulnerable. The dire situation has also affected the health of the population, as the flames and smoke have led to thousands of injuries. The magnitude of the disaster requires urgent attention and support to address the immediate needs of those affected. However, the prevailing weather conditions remain a cause for concern. With temperatures exceeding 45 degrees Celsius and wind speeds exceeding 50 km/h on the Tunisian borders, coupled with low humidity, the conditions were suitable for the expansion and intensification of the wildfires.
Amidst this dire situation, the National Society has been actively engaged in response efforts for several months, successfully completing a significant portion of the distribution operations. Understanding the evolving needs, the National Society has formally requested critical changes from the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), aligning with the adjustments previously outlined.

national_society_actions.title: national_society_eoc
national_society_actions.description:
Immediately following the disaster, an SRC Coordination team was established at SRC HQ to oversee the following activities: 1) Managing the overall SRC response to enhance coordination with Civil Protection needs, requests, SRC teams and other organisations; 2) Coordinating branches, response teams, and the exchange of information with SRC local branch offices, CP authorities, and other partners; 3) Handling logistics, including supporting teams on the sites and transporting donations; 4) Managing information, including reporting and communications; 5) Ensuring safety and security by implementing procedures and providing advice on safety and security related matters; 6) Undertaking all other necessary activities to support the response effort.

After more than two months in the floods response operation, other regular activities also need to be fully addressed again and carried out on a daily basis. Members of the SRC coordination team are still working on the floods response besides their regular duties. 

The logistics department (handling purchases and distribution), financial department, PR department, and coordination of local branches department (also serving as DREF focal point) remain the most active in the floods response operation. The recent floods in October and November intensified the workload of the entire team.

national_society_actions.title: shelter_housing_and_settlements
national_society_actions.description:
SRC provided support to 11 temporary shelters. In these temporary shelter arrangements, the main emphasis was on providing PSS and preventing the separation of family members, including registration processes. The National Society supported families in gathering in a single temporary shelter. SRC volunteers and personnel also offered additional communication tools and services to ensure basic communication between separated family members.

In addition, SRC has supported over 2,000 tourists who were stranded in flooded areas, accommodating them in tourist facilities such as camps, hotels, as well as on highways and regional roads.

IFRC procured and delivered 100 dehumidifiers in September, with an additional 150 units already in operation, funded by other sources. These dehumidifiers have been operational since then, aiding affected populations in dehumidifying flooded infrastructure. The administration of these units is handled by the local branches of the Red Cross.

Furthermore, 250 out of 500 kitchen sets are currently in distribution to meet the needs of 1,500 people, ensuring they have essential household items. This distribution includes food parcels and washing powder to support the affected households.

national_society_actions.title: livelihoods_and_basic_needs
national_society_actions.description:
Due to the impact of floods on markets and stores in rural areas, uncertainty in securing basic everyday items has increased. Considering the high prevalence of social and health-related vulnerabilities in the affected municipalities, the SRC promptly conducted assessments and initiated the distribution of essential items, such as drinking water, food parcels, and hygiene products. Activities related to livelihoods and basic needs in all affected areas were implemented based on requests and coordinated with the Administration for CP and Disaster Relief.

The SRC has distributed over 110 tons of food items, including food parcels, milk, baby foods, and other nutritional items, received as in-kind donations until October. The ongoing distribution includes additional needed food parcels, along with kitchen sets and washing powder.

national_society_actions.title: activation_of_contingency_plans
national_society_actions.description: Immediately after the floods, the CP's flood action plan was activated, and it remained in effect until the end of August. In September, the government passed the "Act on intervention measures to eliminate the consequences of floods and landslides from August 2023."

national_society_actions.title: water_sanitation_and_hygiene
national_society_actions.description:
The SRC provided assistance in the most affected municipalities and communities by supplying drinking water, food parcels, and hygiene kits, primarily sourced from in-kind donations. Activities implemented in all affected areas were carried out based on requests and coordinated with the Administration for CP and Disaster Relief. SRC volunteers have been actively assisting the affected population by cleaning homes, disinfecting, clearing yards, and removing debris. The SRC equipped the affected population with rubber boots and other personal protective equipment (PPE) through material donations from the public.

As of 18 October, the SRC has distributed over 150,000 liters of bottled water and beverages, over 35 tons of hygiene items (many of them donated in-kind to SRC), and has distributed over 4,000 liters of disinfectant liquid. Additionally, the government has provided many disinfection kits and services.

national_society_actions.title: health
national_society_actions.description:
SRC First Aid (FA) team members provided FA to all first responders and personnel engaged in the response, many of whom were themselves affected by the disaster. In addition to FA, SRC FA team members offered psychological first aid (PFA) and psychosocial support (PSS) in the field, with a focus on hard-to-reach households, temporary accommodation centres, and those in vulnerable situations.

Volunteers from the local branches of the SRC are also offering PFA each time they come into contact with affected people, primarily during distribution efforts.

After the initial response, SRC established PFA teams of volunteers from other local branches. There volunteers were already engaged in providing PFA as part of their regular volunteer work or were members of FA Teams involved in previous disaster responses. Before being deployed, volunteers attend a PFA course. 

The PFA team members conducted house-to-house visits in the middle of August. Since then, they have been conducting follow-up visits in the newly affected areas, starting in November. 

The feedback and experience gathered highlight a notable increase in anxiety among affected populations, mostly stemming from urgent needs resulting from the the floods and the impeding winter season. It is evident that the demand for PFA will increase in the upcoming months due to the cold weather.

national_society_actions.title: protection_gender_and_inclusion
national_society_actions.description:
The Child Safeguarding Risk Analysis is being completed in collaboration with the IFRC Regional Office for Europe (ROE). Referral pathways for unaccompanied and separated children (UASC) are established in accordance with national legislation, designating the Centers of Social Work as the responsible authority. Temporary shelters managed by SRC have implemented registration and monitoring procedures to identify and address protection risks.

In mid-September, SRC has opened an additional two-way communication channel - a telephone helpline for anyone in need of support or information, including needs and feedback on PGI. The new call handling system, EspoCRM, was utilised by the SRC call center to file, record, refer, track, and trace feedback. While most calls were about inquiries on how to receive financial aid, it is noteworthy that questions on financial support were not always the main reason for calling. Most of the time, people were seeking for PFA support, which was provided by the call center members.

national_society_actions.title: multi_purpose_cash
national_society_actions.description:
As a result of the rapid assessment, the need to provide cash and voucher assistance for aﬀected households was identified. The flooding and landslides have led to the loss or severe damage of households, including critical elements such as floors, walls, electricity, water, and sanitation facilities. 

These damages include full housing structures, appliances, furniture, agricultural crops, as well as livestock. Consequently, populations in vulnerable situations are unable to cover their basic needs. Through the utilization of multi-purpose cash (MPC) assistance, the SRC can offer additional support to the affected people who are either at or below the poverty line. While SRC currently does not have an agreement in place with a Financial Service Provider (FSP), it has good experience and has previously cooperated with an FSP for gift card assistance. 

The government supported aﬀected households according to the level of damage that was assessed by local damage assessment commissions. The SRC was part of this large-scale, multi-agency cash and voucher (CVA) response programme amounting to EUR 10 million, supported by the Government of Slovenia. The SRC transferred EUR 5,001,044 to 4,419 bank accounts of selected people in vulnerable situations.

Since the beginning of the floods the most affected local branches distributed EUR 1 million via supermarket gift cards, each worth EUR 50.

national_society_actions.title: national_society_readiness
national_society_actions.description:
The SRC consistently monitors the situation in Slovenia and promptly responds to significant emergencies as they arise, regardless of whether an official state of emergency has been declared. 

Recent instances include the rapid response to severe hailstorms in mid-July 2023, floods in August, and at the end of October. All actions undertaken by the SRC are closely coordinated with the Administration for Civil Protection and Disaster Relief.

The SRC immediately responded to this emergency with the deployment of volunteers and staff (primarily from local branches), FA Team members, emergency temporary shelter units, Restoring Family Links (RFL) and PSS teams and volunteers.

A Training of Trainers (ToT) for PFA volunteers is currently in the planning process and will take place in January 2024 to increase local capacity. IFRC is likely to provide support for this event by deploying PGI experts.

national_society_actions.title: assessment
national_society_actions.description:
The SRC conducted an initial needs assessment by creating a customized questionnaire and distributing it to the local branches. Mobilized volunteers have actively collected and continue to gather preliminary data. The data was collected from local branches in a hybrid mode, through the questionnaire, emails, and via phone calls. Additional efforts are necessary to gain a comprehensive humanitarian overview.  

Assessments can be accessed through the following websites:

- Slovenia: Floods IFRC GO page: https://go.ifrc.org/emergencies/6576/additional-info/additional-information

- Slovenia: Floods SRC Damage Assessment dashboard: https://app.powerbi.com/view?r=eyJrIjoiZDQ5NzM1MzEtNmQwMC00Zjc5LWI4NDItYjFiZTM5OTlmOTU2IiwidCI6ImEyYjUzYmU1LTczNGUtNGU2Yy1hYjBkLWQxODRmNjBmZDkxNyIsImMiOjh9

Feedback, experience, and additional unstructured assessments during the operation showed that the approaching winter, coupled with challenging early recovery conditions (where the demand for heavy repair on houses and flats remains high), along with other unmet needs, have heightened the overall needs gap of the affected population for the coming months until the end of winter/end of April.

national_society_actions.title: coordination
national_society_actions.description:
According to National Disaster Response Law, the SRC Secretary General is a part of the National Civil Protection Headquarters to enhance cooperation between CP Authorities and Red Cross. The aim of the cooperation is to minimize the impact of disasters on the population and to support CP with the procurement and delivery of humanitarian aid to the affected population. 

Following the procedure, the internal coordination team within SRC was established. This team is responsible for collecting information on preliminary assessments and expertise on the emergency from SRC Disaster Management (DM), FA, RFL, PSS, Logistics/Supply, Legal, Public Relations (PR), and Information Management focal points. The purpose is to establish a link between Civil Protection and SRC, ensuring a constant exchange of information, needs, reports, and activities in the field. 
Since the end of august 

SRC Headquarters (HQ) organizes regular meetings with local branch offices. SRC has activated internal procedures for communication and coordination within the SRC structure. Following these procedures, local branches regularly send reports to the HQ on conducted activities and needs assessed during field visits. Over time, the number of meetings and reports has been adjusted and reduced based on the evolving needs. Currently, most coordination between the SRC and SRC local branches in affected areas takes place through telephone and email communication.

Coordination by the CP concluded at the end of August and was assumed by the Governmental Working Group for the Coordination of Reconstruction. SRC is actively cooperating with this working group. Additionally, SRC reports and coordinates its PFA activities with the Ministry of Health as part of the National Mental Health programs.

national_society_actions.title: resource_mobilization
national_society_actions.description:
The SRC initiated a domestic resource mobilization campaign, collecting both in-kind donations and funding specifically designated for the implementation of response activities. Relying on funding obtained from private donors, RCRC partners, a government grant earmarked to cash distribution, and through this DREF, the SRC undertook a large-scale response operation. 

A National Society Response Plan is currently being developed to present a comprehensive strategy with a funding ask that includes recovery, long-term support to the population, as well as NS capacity strengthening to be able to deliver specialized and at-scale services. The plan also aims to strengthen the National Society position and auxiliary role. The SRC has not  received funding via the EU response mechanism.

needs_identified.title: protection_gender_and_inclusion
needs_identified.description: Due to the damaged infrastructure of mobile telecommunication networks, especially in difficult-to-access households, and a high number of individuals losing their homes and staying in collective accommodation facilities or with family/friends, there was a crucial need to maintain and restore family links. This needs was supported via various communication channels, including the assistance of RFL team members in securing internet connections and other tools for communication between family members.

needs_identified.title: health
needs_identified.description:
As a result of the disaster, people aﬀected are facing increased stress, fear, and fatigue. Additionally, there is a need to raise awareness related to water-borne diseases, which pose a significant risk to health and well-being during and after ﬂoods. The SRC plans to provide ongoing PFA and PSS activities to aﬀected populations, as well as to Red Cross volunteers and staﬀ engaged in the response operation, while conducting awareness raising activities. These activities were implemented in all affected regions according to the needs. 

In addition to the Tomlin region being heavily affected at the end of October, strong rains also impacted the areas affected in August 2023. 
Based on reports from local branches, the PFA needs of the existing target group (impacted in August) are expected to increase again in the coming months due to the extraordinary heavy rain at the end of October, further worsening the already poor situation. 

In November, all local branches from affected areas requested follow-up visits and additional PSS activities, specially targeting children aged 13 to 16 years old and older people. In addition to PSS activities, SRC will focus on training volunteers to enhance local capacity in PSS and promote awareness of water safety.

needs_identified.title: livelihoods_and_basic_needs
needs_identified.description:
In August many households are working on their agricultural infrastructure, home gardens, and land, which are essential sources for their basic food needs. Due to the damage caused to these lands and its impact on access to food, there is a need to support the most aﬀected families with food parcels and/ or cash support. 

Despite the initial response (multi purpose cash grants, food parcels, gift cards, etc.) to address the most urgent needs, people still require food and other basic support. Although the government and NGOs are assisting affected populations, people in vulnerable situations still lack sufficient means to recover - especially due to the challenging recovery conditions (mainly meteorologically triggered) and the current winter season. Local branches have also reported that companies severely impacted by the floods are now dismissing people. As a consequence, challenges are increasing in affected areas, impacting both affected and non-affected populations.

needs_identified.title: water_sanitation_and_hygiene
needs_identified.description:
Local branches have reported a demand for everyday hygiene, cleaning, and washing items, including washing powder. This need arises from a general rise in prices and the limited financial resources of affected households. Repairs and renovations are generally expensive and place a burden on household budgets.

Moreover, there is a potential for increased interest in future preparedness activities, particularly in acquiring additional knowledge on basic hygiene promotion and household water treatment.

needs_identified.title: shelter_housing_and_settlements
needs_identified.description:
As a result of a rapid needs assessment and information collected from branches and CP authorities, it has been identify that there is significant damage to homes. Aﬀected households required support with: 1) Cleaning, disinfecting, and dehumidifying flooded homes and businesses; 2) Information and assistance for recovery; 3) Basic household items to recover lost assets, including those needed for response and self-recovery, such as cleaning tools and rubber boots.

In order to ensure continued support in the upcoming months, the following items require replenishment: household items and flood protection equipment.

One community has been relocated after four months because the Government identified the area where they were located as non-safe.

In general, and based on local branch feedback after the initial response and support the families in vulnerable situations are still in need of household and cleaning items.

planned_interventions.progress_towards_outcome:
PFA was provided to people during all types of distribution (food, essential relief items, and gift cards) as well as during other face-to-face activates. The needs for PFA were high, especially in the first two months of the response,  and remain high since. To meet these needs, the SRC PFA team was established to focus solely on PFA support. Thanks to the timeframe extension of the DREF operation, PFA support activities will continue until the end of the winter season/end of March/April.

From mid-August until the end of September, teams for PFA support were conducting house  visits, reaching 1,212 persons. At the beginning of the response, PFA activities were financially supported by the Government.

In addition to follow up visits in areas affected by the August floods, Red Cross PFA teams are conducting house visits to household in Tolminsko affected by the October/November events. Furthermore, PFA support was also provided in the SRC call centre. Mobilisation of volunteers for PFA services has been supported by vehicles VRP covered under DREF.

On the second page of website, the needs reported via local branches in the first month of the response can be accessed: https://app.powerbi.com/view?r=eyJrIjoiZDQ5NzM1MzEtNmQwMC00Zjc5LWI4NDItYjFiZTM5OTlmOTU2IiwidCI6ImEyYjUzYmU1LTczNGUtNGU2Yy1hYjBkLWQxODRmNjBmZDkxNyIsImMiOjh9. 

The generally challenging situation (e.g. weather, new disaster events) after the summer floods and as it is still unclear for some people whether they permanently have to leave their houses and start full renovation, recovery activities have slowed down. Most recovery construction work will start in the spring of 2024. As the number of injuries at home is almost seven times higher as at the workplace and the risk of injuries is expected to be even higher during the renovation of apartments, to ensure a safe environment during house renovations, SRC will purchase and distribute first aid kits for a targeted 300 households. The distribution of first aid kits replaces the distribution of hygiene related clothing items.

planned_interventions.description: Distribution of vouchers to the affected population Organise post–distribution monitoring. 1,000 HHs will be selected based on vulneratbility criteria that is co-ordinated with other sectoral services and services by authorities. Voucher value per household will vary depending on applicability of vulnerability criteria. Commodity suppliers will be identified based on availability in the most affected areas, where voucher distribution will be implemented as complementary assistance. Complementarity will also be observed in relation to the timeline, and gaps and residual needs following multi purpose cash distri-bution funded via government sources. There will be checks in place to mitigate fraud risk, with validation process in place. Selection will be done through local committees consisting of multiple NGO and local municipality actors, along centrally defined criteria, that will be harmonized with the multi purpose cash programmes. As the programme is in cooperation with the ministry, personal identities and individ- ual pre-existing vulnerabilities (pre-existing reliance on the social services ) will be verified.
